title: Neuro-Oncology Fellowship
prerequisites: Learner: licensed physician or senior neurology/oncology trainee; conceptual course assumes completed core neurology, neuroanatomy, oncology principles, neuroimaging basics, pathology/molecular biology and evidence appraisal. This course grants no qualification.
Review WHO CNS5 summary and basic MRI sequences before Units 2–3.
Familiarity with clinical trial design and adult/pediatric distinctions is helpful.
objectives: Apply the published UCNS blueprint as an educational map: adult primary tumors 35%, pediatric primary tumors 25%, metastases 15%, systemic cancer-related neurologic disorders 25%.
Reason from presentation and diagnostic studies to integrated histomolecular diagnosis while exposing uncertainty.
Compare current evidence and guideline recommendations for primary and metastatic CNS tumors without giving patient-specific orders.
Recognize neurologic emergencies and the need for multidisciplinary escalation.
Discuss supportive care, trial methods and evidence limitations.

assignment.title: Integrated case conference portfolio (fictional cases only)
deliverables: Write a 1-page structured consult note using an explicitly fictional case: problem representation, localization, differential, immediate safety concerns, diagnostic plan, multidisciplinary roles, uncertainty.
Prepare a one-page integrated tumor-board summary interpreting hypothetical histology and molecular data; list missing tests and avoid conclusions unsupported by the data.
Compare two guideline-supported options for a fictional patient using evidence quality, benefits/harms, patient goals, eligibility limits and date checked.
Appraise one neuro-oncology trial abstract with PICO, primary endpoint, safety, bias, generalizability and consent considerations.
Submit a 500-word reflective note on limits of self-study and a personal update plan.
assignment.passThreshold: Not a validated competency or board predictor. Suggested self-study completion threshold: 80/100 plus all safety-critical items correctly identified; no formal credential.

assessment.format: 10 original questions in this packet plus unit retrieval quizzes, case conference assignment and evidence appraisal.
rubric: Correct identification of blueprint domain and evidence source.
Differential and diagnostic reasoning distinguish suspected imaging diagnosis from confirmed integrated diagnosis.
Therapeutic answers include qualifiers, contraindications/uncertainty and date/source.
Safety answers identify urgent escalation and avoid self-directed treatment.
assessment.limitations: Not official UCNS/ABMS content, not a validated exam predictor, and not a substitute for clinical evaluation or human assessment.

topicGaps: The 36h free-video target remains unmet: 10.467h verified from 11 unique videos/explicit instructional segments; 25.533h remains. New videos add 7.550h, but do not close the residual gap.

Coverage is improved for pediatric glioma classification and low-grade glioma, PCNSL overview, insular glioma, neurologist-facing emergency recognition, trial conversations, adult glioma molecular profiling, and supportive/survivorship foundations. Patient/caregiver or nursing education is separately categorized as foundation, not physician-level specialty didactics.

Inadequate publicly verified full-length instruction remains for pediatric high-grade/embryonal/germ-cell tumors, pediatric neurocutaneous/familial syndromes and developmental follow-up, PCNSL full professional diagnostic and therapeutic reasoning, leptomeningeal/epidural/plexus/peripheral-nerve metastases, radiation necrosis and RANO case application, immunotherapy/CAR-T neurotoxicity, infection/vasculopathy/VTE, rare adult CNS tumors, palliative care, and advanced clinical-trial methods.

Several eligible recordings are dated, broad, or patient-facing. Current guidelines and source dates must be checked before relying on a therapeutic or eligibility statement; recording access and duration do not certify factual currency.

SNO Academy pages describe on-demand CME content whose access may be member-gated; it was not counted or accessed behind a login. The SIOP targeted-pediatric-glioma candidate was unavailable at its direct watch URL when checked and was not counted. No complete free public professional lecture archive is evidenced by the official programme pages.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: United Council for Neurologic Subspecialties (UCNS) Neuro-oncology certification examination
American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) primary specialty certification (neurology/child neurology) where applicable
American Board of Neurological Surgery (ABNS) primary specialty certification where applicable
American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) medical oncology primary specialty certification where applicable
American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) pediatric hematology-oncology primary specialty certification where applicable
American Board of Radiology (ABR) radiation oncology primary specialty certification where applicable
Equivalent Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada (RCPSC) or American Osteopathic Association (AOA) primary specialty certification where accepted by UCNS
medical.boardStatus: The UCNS offers a separate neuro-oncology subspecialty certification examination (200 multiple-choice items, four hours; exam offered biennially in odd-numbered years). UCNS explains that its emerging neurologic subspecialty certifications are for fields too small to meet ABMS subspecialty-recognition requirements; the current ABMS certificate list does not include neuro-oncology. Primary specialty board certification/equivalent and an eligible pathway are required; training alone does not confer eligibility. AAN public directory marks the MGB/DFCI programme UCNS-approved and not ACGME-approved. The dynamic UCNS directory itself did not render a program-specific result in public static extraction; the AAN record supplies the current program-level UCNS approval statement.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: UCNS eligibility is subject to its current criteria and applicant pathway. Current criteria require an appropriate primary board certification/equivalent and unrestricted medical license, plus one of the specified UCNS pathways; the accredited-fellowship pathway requires successful completion of a UCNS-accredited 12+ month neuro-oncology fellowship and application within 48 months. The official MGB page describes one clinical year plus 1–2 optional research years, but applicants must confirm that their exact appointment/cohort and full completion record meet current UCNS requirements. The MGB page lists neurology as the expected pathway and other specialties case-by-case. This independent course confers no eligibility.

officialProgrammes.name: MGH-DFCI-BWH Neuro-Oncology Fellowship (MGB directory variant: MGB Neuro-oncology Fellowship; MGH GME variant: MGH Neuro-Oncology Fellowship Program)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The official programme states it is a jointly recruited clinical neuro-oncology cohort among MGH, DFCI and BWH, established in 2003; one clinical year plus 1–2 optional research years, with a broad case mix including primary tumors, CNS lymphoma, metastases and treatment complications. It says four trainees per year and an expected neurology-residency/ABPN qualification, with other specialties considered case-by-case. MGH page says BWH/MGH rotations start July 2028. The AAN page describes one year, states UCNS approval Yes and ACGME approval No. It is a real clinical physician fellowship, not a generic directory category or exclusively research/postdoctoral offering; optional research years are distinct.

officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Institutional variant kept separate from the MGB Neurology Fellowship directory entry. medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet includes the MGB and MGH official pages. Their descriptions show two directory/hosting variants of one jointly recruited MGH-DFCI-BWH-HMS clinical fellowship, not separate adult and pediatric programmes. UCNS requirements require pediatric-specific instruction (at least two weeks) within fellowship curriculum; the MGH/DFCI/BWH public overview does not publish a detailed rotation schedule or a separate pediatric track. Optional research years are research supplements to a clinical physician fellowship, not a separate board-recognized specialty. NIH research postdoctoral fellowships are not included as a clinical physician programme. No separate ABMS neuro-oncology board was identified; UCNS subspecialty exam is separate from primary specialty boards.
sourceCaveats: The UCNS directory page uses a dynamic search and did not render program-specific rows in stateless fetch; the AAN public listing states UCNS Approval: Yes and ACGME Approval: No. Do not infer from the directory shell alone.

The PCNSL EHA-ESMO article fetch returned an anti-bot interstitial. It was not opened through authenticated/shared browser or bypassed; link is retained as a source lead, not as a verified detailed recommendation source.
The 2025 FDA prescribing label PDF fetch did not extract text, so the report avoids quoting dosing and asks learners to verify label/current safety before any care decision.

Official programme pages do not publish a full didactic lecture archive, detailed month-by-month curriculum, full case counts or patient volume. Do not infer volumes or guaranteed eligibility from promotional descriptions.
The official MGB page says four trainees yearly; AAN directory says three to four. Report as a public-source discrepancy, not a reconciled cohort number.
No human clinical review was performed. This is independent education and not affiliation, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence or certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult diffuse glioma is IDH-mutant and 1p/19q codeleted. Which WHO CNS5 entity best fits this integrated profile?

options.text: Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted
Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype
Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered

practiceQuestions.rationale: The adult-type diffuse glioma category defined by IDH mutation plus whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion is oligodendroglioma. Histology and grade still matter; no isolated radiographic appearance replaces integrated diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which finding can support a glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype CNS WHO grade 4 designation in an adult diffuse astrocytic tumor even without classic necrosis/microvascular proliferation?

options.text: TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or +7/−10 in the appropriate context
MGMT promoter methylation alone
ATRX loss alone
A single enhancing MRI lesion

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO CNS5 permits molecular criteria including TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or +7/−10 in the correct adult IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic setting. This is not a stand-alone shortcut without the right diagnostic context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with resected grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma is being considered for deferring RT/chemotherapy. Which 2025 ASCO-SNO update is relevant to discuss as an option when RT/chemotherapy is deferred?

options.text: Vorasidenib may be offered in the defined grade 2 IDH-mutant setting
Vorasidenib is mandatory for every IDH-mutant glioma
Bevacizumab is standard for all low-grade gliomas
Temozolomide is contraindicated

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 rapid update states vorasidenib may be offered to selected grade 2 IDH-mutant astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma when further RT and chemotherapy have been or can be deferred; it is conditional, not universal.

practiceQuestions.stem: For glioblastoma with equivocal MRI change within 12 weeks after radiotherapy, what RANO 2.0 principle applies when clinical status permits?

options.text: Consider continuation with confirmatory MRI or unequivocal histopathology before calling progression
Call progression on enhancement alone
Ignore clinical status and use a single scan
Use only preoperative scan as the baseline in all settings

practiceQuestions.rationale: RANO 2.0 notes pseudoprogression is common in the first 12 weeks after RT; confirm progression by repeat imaging, or unequivocal histopathology, before defining progression. Clinical judgment remains essential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with a newly diagnosed brain tumor has never had a seizure. What does the SNO/EANO guideline recommend for routine primary seizure prophylaxis?

options.text: Do not prescribe antiseizure medication solely to reduce first seizure risk
Start levetiracetam for every patient
Start valproate to prolong survival
Use prophylaxis if lesion is frontal

practiceQuestions.rationale: The SNO/EANO guideline recommends against prescribing antiepileptic drugs to reduce seizure risk in newly diagnosed brain tumor patients with no seizure history (Level A). Perioperative questions have separate uncertainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the UCNS neuro-oncology exam blueprint weight for metastatic cancer to the nervous system?
practiceQuestions.rationale: The UCNS content outline assigns 15% to metastatic cancer to the nervous system, with brain/spinal cord, skull base, leptomeningeal, epidural, plexus/peripheral nerve and cord-compression subdomains.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which best distinguishes MGH-DFCI-BWH programme structure from its optional research years?

options.text: One clinical year is described; years two and three are optional research-focused, not a substitute for clinical fellowship core
The entire programme is research-only
The public page documents three compulsory clinical years
The 2028 rotation change already governs all cohorts

practiceQuestions.rationale: The MGB programme page describes one clinical year plus 1–2 optional research years, with research activity devoted to lab/translational/clinical research; it separately notes rotations across MGH and BWH starting July 2028.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which organization certifies the neuro-oncology subspecialty examination described in this course?

options.text: UCNS
ABPN as a separate ABMS neuro-oncology subspecialty board
ACGME
SF Match

practiceQuestions.rationale: UCNS offers the neuro-oncology subspecialty certification exam. Applicants must also meet primary specialty board certification and licensure criteria; SF Match is the match organizer and ACGME is an accreditor, not this certifier.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the best teaching use of TCIA TCGA-GBM imaging data?

options.text: Access the de-identified images under collection rules, cite the dataset, and do not republish images without confirming permissions
Assume public download means unrestricted image republication
Link images to real identities using matched clinical records
Copy images into course files without checking controlled-access flags

practiceQuestions.rationale: TCIA describes de-identified imaging and requires dataset citation/usage-policy compliance; some data may be controlled due to face reconstruction risk. Public view/download is not permission to republish.

practiceQuestions.stem: A suspected PCNSL case raises a treatment and diagnostic sequencing question. What is the appropriate learning response?

options.text: Use current PCNSL guideline and coordinate urgently with relevant neuro-oncology, hematology/oncology, neuroradiology and neuropathology; do not infer diagnosis from imaging alone
Assume glioblastoma based on enhancement
Use the older guideline as an immutable directive
Offer a specific dose from this educational module

practiceQuestions.rationale: PCNSL is a distinct disease with guideline-specific diagnosis and therapy; imaging alone is not definitive, and clinicians must consult current sources and multidisciplinary colleagues. This item tests safe reasoning, not treatment.

unitMap.text: Core principles, dose-response, risk and pharmacokinetics
coveredTopics: Hazard versus risk; concentration/effect; receptor mechanisms; ADME; developmental and reproductive toxicology; sources and uncertainty.

unitMap.text: First-hour assessment, toxidromes and stabilization
coveredTopics: Airway/breathing/circulation, temperature, glucose, ECG, pupils/secretions/skin, co-ingestions, poison-center consultation, decontamination safety.

unitMap.text: Common prescription and OTC medication poisonings
coveredTopics: Acetaminophen, salicylates, opioids, sedative-hypnotics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, cardiovascular drugs; poison center referral.

unitMap.text: Toxidromes, autonomic agents, stimulants and serotonin-related emergencies
coveredTopics: Cholinesterase inhibitors, sympathomimetics, serotonin toxicity, NMS differential, withdrawal, toxidrome caveats.

unitMap.text: Toxic alcohols, caustics and household agents
coveredTopics: Methanol, ethylene glycol, isopropanol, hydrocarbons, caustics, cleaning products, gaps and assay timing.

unitMap.text: Antidotes, decontamination and enhanced elimination
coveredTopics: Activated charcoal, selected decontamination, antidote mechanisms, dialysis principles, evidence and poison-center/toxicologist consultation.

unitMap.text: Analytical, forensic and workplace drug testing
coveredTopics: Immunoassay screening limits, confirmatory mass spectrometry, specimen interpretation, chain of custody, medicolegal/ethical issues.

unitMap.text: Environmental and occupational toxicology
coveredTopics: CO, lead, mercury, solvents, pesticides, indoor air, dose/pathway, community and workplace determinants.

unitMap.text: Metals, gases, radiation and chemical/biological emergencies
coveredTopics: Metals/metalloids, asphyxiants, radiation principles, chemical warfare agents, biological exposures, CHEMM resources.

unitMap.text: Natural toxins, supplements, foodborne toxins and envenomations
coveredTopics: Plants, mushrooms, marine/fish toxins, envenomations, foodborne toxins, supplements, counterfeit and unregulated products.

unitMap.text: Substance use, addiction toxicology and poisoning prevention
coveredTopics: Opioids, stimulants, sedatives, novel psychoactive substances, alcohols, withdrawal, naloxone context, prevention systems.

unitMap.text: Integrative cases, population health, scholarship and administration
coveredTopics: Consultation practice; poison-center administration; ToxIC/surveillance concepts; case conference; research methods; ethics; systems practice.

topicGaps: Principles/toxicokinetics: one acid-base/electrolyte lecture added; broad dose-response, toxicokinetics, developmental/reproductive toxicology and molecular mechanisms remain undercovered.
Initial clinical assessment and toxidromes: no new complete first-hour stabilization/toxidrome recording verified.
Medication overdoses and antidotes: one immunotherapy adverse-effect lecture added; common acute overdose classes, antidotes and current protocol-level instruction remain incomplete.
Toxic alcohols and household chemicals: no new verified full recording found; EXTRIP web recommendations support source-linked study but are not hours of video.
Analytical and forensic toxicology: drug-facilitated amnesia lecture adds context, but validated assay selection, detection windows, confirmation and chain-of-custody instruction remain incomplete.
Environmental and occupational exposure: no new verified full recording found; CO and exposure-history instruction remains reading-based.
Chemical/radiological emergencies: no new verified full recording found; incident command, responder safety, radiological principles and agent-specific preparation remain reading/resource gaps.
Natural toxins and envenomation: no new verified full recording found.
Addiction/substance-use toxicology: no new verified full recording found; medication treatment, withdrawal and prevention topics remain gaps.

Population health, poison-center administration and scholarship: one relevant NYC poison-center-affiliated teaching set is available, but surveillance, QI, administration and research methods remain undercovered.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The supplied MGB packet variant, current BCH programme page, Mass./RI Poison Center page, older programme PDF, and ACMT listing were compared. This is a physician clinical subspecialty fellowship (not a generic non-physician toxicology course, PhD/research-only fellowship, or identified combined fellowship). It is distinct from primary residency. Official current public pages establish a two-year clinical fellowship and named clinical/didactic activities. ACGME requirements were reviewed, but the ACGME public data portal’s individual-program record was not retrieved; do not claim institution-level accreditation or current accreditation status from the generic requirements or a directory listing. The separate board exam is real and is administered by ABEM.
sourceCaveats: Institution pages disagree on their named affiliation lists and on which residency backgrounds may apply; preserve the exact variant and verify current program instructions directly.

The MGB source reports 250–300 in-person consultations and around 46,000 center calls in calendar year 2025; ACMT page reports a nearby but different number (45,000). These public statistics are not independently audited, not a current case-volume guarantee, and are not instructional credit. Not used as curricular requirements.
ACGME national program requirements support national training structure only. Individual Harvard/MGB/BCH program accreditation was not confirmed from ACGME public program data.
The ABEM web page contains date-sensitive 2026 exam information; current board rules and the cross-board pathway must be checked directly before applying.
Several free-to-view slides/PDFs are not licensed for republication. This curriculum links only and rehosts no source content, clinical images, patient records or cases.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 38-year-old reports that headaches and nausea recur at home on weekends; a household member reports similar symptoms. Which next step best tests the exposure hypothesis?

options.text: A. Attribute symptoms to migraine because examination is normal
B. Obtain a focused environmental/work exposure timeline and assess for carbon monoxide exposure with appropriate confirmatory testing
C. Order a routine urine drug immunoassay as a comprehensive toxin screen
D. Exclude a toxic exposure if a household member has no symptoms

practiceQuestions.rationale: A cluster and temporal pattern should prompt an exposure history and directed evaluation. A normal exam or broad immunoassay does not rule out environmental exposure.
practiceQuestions.originalityNote: Original educational item written for this independent course; not official/proprietary board content.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with suspected carbon monoxide exposure has a normal conventional two-wavelength pulse-oximeter reading. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: A. This excludes clinically important carbon monoxide exposure
B. Conventional two-wavelength pulse oximetry is unreliable when carboxyhemoglobin is present; assess exposure history and measure carboxyhemoglobin by co-oximetry
C. It proves the patient has methemoglobinemia
D. It determines the severity and outcome of exposure

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC warns that ordinary two-wavelength pulse oximetry is not accurate with COHb; blood CO-oximetry is used to confirm, and COHb concentration correlates poorly with severity/outcomes.
practiceQuestions.originalityNote: Original educational item written for this independent course; not official/proprietary board content.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient arrives 2.5 hours after a reported single acetaminophen ingestion. The initial concentration is below the nomogram treatment line. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: A. Use the value to rule out toxicity because it is below the line
B. A concentration obtained before 4 hours cannot be plotted to risk-stratify on the nomogram; obtain an appropriately timed concentration and apply the consensus pathway
C. Ignore timing and initiate dialysis
D. The nomogram applies equally to repeated supratherapeutic ingestion

practiceQuestions.rationale: The consensus statement specifies that a sample before 4 hours post-ingestion cannot be used to risk-stratify with the nomogram; repeated ingestion and unreliable history require different pathways.
practiceQuestions.originalityNote: Original educational item written for this independent course; not official/proprietary board content.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with possible chronic salicylate toxicity is confused, volume depleted and has a salicylate concentration that is not markedly elevated. Which principle is most important?

options.text: A. The acute-ingestion nomogram determines chronic toxicity severity
B. Interpret the level with acuity, clinical condition and acid-base status; do not rely on the acute nomogram or the concentration alone
C. A falling level always indicates improvement
D. Do not contact nephrology until a fixed number is exceeded

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACMT emphasizes context, repeated levels, acid-base status and clinical course; the Done nomogram is not reliable in acute or chronic poisoning. The source is a 2013 position paper, so contemporary specialist consultation is required.
practiceQuestions.originalityNote: Original educational item written for this independent course; not official/proprietary board content.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has a positive point-of-care urine immunoassay for a drug class but no compatible clinical syndrome. What is the strongest conclusion?

options.text: A. Exposure and current impairment are proved
B. The assay result must be interpreted according to assay cross-reactivity, detection window and clinical context; confirmatory testing may be needed
C. A negative result would exclude all members of the class
D. The result establishes dose and timing

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening immunoassays do not establish dose, timing, current impairment or all agents in a class. The Core Content includes analytical and forensic interpretation, not uncritical interpretation of screens.
practiceQuestions.originalityNote: Original educational item written for this independent course; not official/proprietary board content.

practiceQuestions.stem: At a suspected unknown chemical incident, responders observe symptomatic people near a release. What is the correct first systems-level priority?

options.text: A. Enter the suspected release zone to identify the product
B. Protect responder safety, establish incident coordination and safe zones, then use hazard-specific clinical/decontamination guidance
C. Collect patient belongings before isolation
D. Assume a specific agent from one nonspecific symptom

practiceQuestions.rationale: CHEMM directs scene size-up, responder safety, incident command/control zones, then agent-specific clinical care. Identification should not precede safe response.

deliverables: Select one emergency ultrasound application and define indications, exclusions and escalation criteria from current guidance.

assessment.format: Twelve unit formative case/checklist submissions; 10 original single-best-answer questions; final QA/teaching charter.
assessment.suggestedCompletionStandard: Self-study target: 80% on original formative questions after feedback and completion of all written submissions; this is not a validated exam threshold, clinical competency assessment, credential or predictor of passing.
assessment.studyPlan: Suggested study plan only: 10 hours per unit across free readings, note-taking, guided image review, simulation planning and assessments; exact learner time varies. This is not video time or supervised clinical practice.

studyHours.basis: Self-study allocation of approximately 10 hours per unit. Estimated planning time, not external recorded media.

unitMap.text: Physics, instrumentation, ergonomics and safety
coveredTopics: Explain pulse-echo, frequency, attenuation, resolution, Doppler and common artifacts.
Select transducer, depth, gain, focus and presets; optimize the image systematically.
Recognize ALARA and the limits of bedside scans.
Transducer frequency, penetration and spatial-resolution trade-offs; linear, curvilinear and phased-array selection by target depth and field of view.
Depth, overall gain, time-gain compensation, focal zone and preset as separate optimization controls; change one control at a time.
Reverberation, acoustic shadowing/enhancement, mirror artifact, anisotropy and Doppler fundamentals; artifact versus anatomy.
Probe-marker orientation, display convention, patient ergonomics, infection prevention and ALARA/output awareness; ultrasound does not replace definitive imaging.

unitMap.text: Image acquisition, documentation and interpretation framework
coveredTopics: Apply probe orientation, patient positioning and systematic sweeps.
Distinguish inadequate from negative examinations and document indication, findings, limitations and action.
Integrate pretest probability and alternative diagnoses.
Question-first exam design: indication, target anatomy, intended protocol and limits of a negative result.
Transducer/patient positioning, landmark confirmation, systematic sweep, orthogonal planes and saving representative clips.
Quality categories: adequate-positive, adequate-negative within a defined protocol, and limited/nondiagnostic; unseen anatomy is not a negative result.
Structured report: indication, views, image adequacy, findings, limits, integration, communication and escalation; archive/feedback requirements vary by institution.

unitMap.text: Trauma: FAST/eFAST and resuscitation
coveredTopics: Acquire pericardial, RUQ, LUQ, pelvic and pleural views.
Explain false-negative/false-positive causes and why a negative FAST does not exclude injury.
Integrate findings with hemodynamics and trauma pathway; avoid delaying resuscitation.
Pericardial, RUQ, LUQ, pelvic and pleural windows; position-dependent dependent spaces and deliberate probe sweeps.
Free-fluid appearance and anatomic verification; distinguish potential-space fluid from vessel, bowel, cyst or artifact.
Sensitivity constraints: small/early fluid, body habitus, incomplete windows, operator factors and timing; negative FAST does not rule out injury.
eFAST pleural signs and trauma workflow: focused adjunct only, with resuscitation and definitive evaluation taking priority.

unitMap.text: Focused cardiac ultrasound and arrest
coveredTopics: Obtain parasternal long/short, apical four-chamber and subxiphoid windows.
Recognize gross LV function, pericardial effusion/tamponade physiology, RV dilation and standstill with qualifiers.
Use ultrasound during arrest without prolonging pulse checks or interrupting compressions.
Parasternal long/short, apical four-chamber and subxiphoid windows; alternate windows and adequacy limits.
Qualitative gross LV function, chamber size, pericardial effusion and right-heart observations; no substitution for comprehensive echocardiography.
Effusion versus tamponade physiology; RV enlargement/strain is nonspecific and may reflect chronic or alternative causes.
Arrest workflow: pre-position probe/operator, use an established pause protocol, and never prolong a pulse check or interrupt compressions.

unitMap.text: Shock, hemodynamics and integrated RUSH
coveredTopics: Build a structured question-driven shock exam from cardiac, lung, IVC, aortic and abdominal views.
Interpret fluid tolerance/responsiveness cautiously, accounting for ventilation and right-heart pressures.
State what POCUS cannot resolve and what additional testing is needed.
Question-driven sequence across heart, lungs, aorta, abdomen and venous assessment; match views to competing shock mechanisms.
Distinguish observations from inferred physiology; relate focused findings to trajectory and pretest probability.

IVC caliber/variation confounders include ventilation and respiratory effort, right-sided pressure and other cardiac/physiologic factors; no single IVC value is a stand-alone volume or fluid-responsiveness test.
Discordant or limited studies prompt reassessment, qualified consultation or additional testing; do not delay stabilization.

unitMap.text: Pulmonary and airway ultrasound
coveredTopics: Recognize lung sliding, B-lines, pleural fluid, consolidation and pneumothorax signs.
Describe artifacts and competing causes; use a standardized bilateral examination.
Use airway ultrasound as adjunct rather than substitute for waveform capnography.
Pleural line and bat sign; A-line reverberation, B-line criteria/distribution and Z-line distinctions.
Lung sliding, lung pulse, seashore pattern and absent-sliding differential; local sliding argues against pneumothorax only at the sampled site.
Pneumothorax scanning by patient position and nondependent region; recognize subcutaneous emphysema, pleural fluid, low ventilation and other technical/clinical pitfalls.
Diffuse versus focal B-line patterns are not etiology-specific; integrate with cardiac and clinical assessment. Airway ultrasound is adjunctive and does not replace waveform capnography.

unitMap.text: Aorta, vascular access and DVT
coveredTopics: Measure abdominal aorta in appropriate transverse/longitudinal planes and identify limits.
Perform compression-based proximal DVT assessment at the defined protocol level.
Differentiate artery/vein and describe dynamic needle visualization, sterile technique and complication awareness.
Aortic transverse and longitudinal survey, measurement plane and outer-wall convention per the selected local protocol; incomplete aortic visualization cannot exclude aneurysm.
Compression ultrasound at protocol-defined proximal venous sites; incompressibility is a finding to interpret with clinical context, not a complete venous survey.
Differentiate artery and vein using anatomy, compressibility and flow characteristics; avoid assuming one cue is definitive.
Procedure planning, sterile field, needle-tip visualization, adjacent-structure awareness and stop/reposition rule when the tip is lost; simulation and supervision required.

unitMap.text: Pregnancy, pelvic and first-trimester ultrasound
coveredTopics: Describe transabdominal/transvaginal use and pregnancy of unknown location framework.
Identify that absence of visible intrauterine pregnancy alone does not prove ectopic pregnancy.
Escalate unstable patients and avoid delaying definitive evaluation.
Transabdominal versus transvaginal approach, indications, consent, scope and technical limitations.
Pregnancy of unknown location: no visible intrauterine pregnancy is not itself proof of ectopic pregnancy; correlate with appropriate follow-up and definitive pathways.
Assess hemodynamic stability and escalation needs before extended image acquisition; avoid delaying urgent evaluation.
Document visualization/adequacy and unresolved location; local follow-up and consultation pathways govern care.

unitMap.text: Biliary, renal and gastrointestinal applications
coveredTopics: Assess gallbladder, biliary tree, hydronephrosis and selected bowel/abdominal findings.
Separate screening/limited POCUS from formal diagnostic imaging.
Recognize non-diagnostic studies and dangerous mimics.
Gallbladder orientation, stones, wall/pericholecystic findings and biliary tree limits; avoid treating one sign as definitive.
Renal collecting-system dilation and bladder assessment; distinguish screening for hydronephrosis/retention from comprehensive urinary imaging.
Selected bowel/abdominal patterns and mimics; indication- and operator-dependent scope.
Nondiagnostic study, dangerous mimics and escalation to formal imaging/consultation when uncertainty remains.

unitMap.text: Soft tissue, MSK, ocular and pediatric extensions
coveredTopics: Characterize superficial collection/cellulitis and selected MSK/ocular indications with scope limits.
Use age-appropriate adaptations and state where pediatric-specific evidence/pathways apply.
Identify high-risk ocular presentations requiring immediate escalation; avoid pressure with suspected globe injury.
Cellulitis-versus-collection patterns and superficial foreign-body assessment with acoustic shadowing/limits.
Selected MSK and ocular indications, standardized orientation and escalation for high-risk findings.
Suspected globe injury: avoid pressure on the globe and obtain urgent qualified assessment; no unsupervised ocular scanning.
Pediatric adaptation: age, cooperation, anatomy and pediatric-specific pathway/evidence; not a separate pediatric clinical authorization.

unitMap.text: Procedural guidance, simulation and competency
coveredTopics: Plan and simulate ultrasound-guided vascular access and drainage with sterile field, continuous needle-tip visualization and safety checks.
Identify contraindications/complications and stop when visualization is inadequate.
Use deliberate practice and direct observation; distinguish knowledge completion from procedural competence.
Pre-procedure question, anatomy, contraindication review, consent, equipment check and simulation rehearsal.
Dynamic in-plane/out-of-plane needle tracking: maintain tip visibility, identify adjacent anatomy, stop if tip is lost and reacquire safely under supervision.
Sterile probe/cable/field practices, complication recognition, post-procedure confirmation and documentation per local policy.
Competency requires repeated deliberate practice and direct observation; knowledge questions, completion certificates and scan counts alone do not establish procedural competence.

unitMap.text: Education, research, QA, administration and leadership
coveredTopics: Design image archive, feedback, QA and peer-review workflows; protect confidentiality.
Critically appraise diagnostic evidence and build a feasible, ethical scholarly question.
Create a teaching session and program implementation plan with equity and resource constraints.
Image archive governance, access control, privacy, retention, feedback turnaround and peer-review workflow.
Image adequacy and interpretation audit, discrepancy review, calibration, escalation and improvement cycles; define denominators and avoid blame-oriented metrics.
Diagnostic-accuracy evidence: population, reference standard, prevalence/spectrum, operator training, uncertainty and transferability.
Ethical feasible study questions, teaching design, faculty development, resource/equity effects and update triggers for evolving guidelines.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The MGB page identifies a real one-year joint physician fellowship, merged as Harvard Emergency Ultrasound Fellowship at MGB in 2021, with MGH and BWH as clinical sites. Institutional curriculum and training expectations are reported only as publicly posted; no clinical training is delivered here. The SCUF program page is a directory entry, not accreditation evidence. The AEMUS FPD is an ABEM credential pathway, not a separate residency or board specialty.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hemodynamically unstable trauma patient has no free fluid on a technically adequate FAST. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Intra-abdominal hemorrhage is excluded.
A negative FAST does not exclude injury or bleeding; continue resuscitation and definitive evaluation based on the full clinical picture.
Repeat only after discharge.
CT is never indicated.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FAST is a focused search for free fluid; sensitivity varies with volume, windows and operator, so a negative examination cannot rule out injury. [ACEP FAST guidance].

practiceQuestions.stem: During cardiac arrest a learner proposes a prolonged ultrasound examination to search for reversible causes. Best safety response?

options.text: Continue uninterrupted until all windows are obtained.
Obtain focused imaging only within the resuscitation workflow without extending pauses or delaying compressions.
Stop CPR while measuring EF.
Use ultrasound to independently terminate resuscitation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ultrasound must not delay chest compressions or lengthen pulse checks; its use is adjunctive and operator/workflow dependent.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with suspected PE has RV dilation on focused cardiac US. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: RV dilation confirms acute PE.
The finding may support RV pressure/volume strain and severity assessment but is not sensitive/specific enough alone to diagnose PE; consider chronic disease and confirmatory pathway.
It excludes PE if absent.
TAPSE is a definitive PE test.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACEP Sonoguide explicitly cautions that RV strain alone is not sensitive for PE and can be chronic; POCUS informs but does not replace diagnostic pathways.

practiceQuestions.stem: On lung ultrasound, absent sliding is seen in one anterior zone. What next?

options.text: Call pneumothorax as proven.
Check image quality and seek additional signs/context; absent sliding has other causes and is not by itself specific.
Assume normal because sliding is variable.
Treat based solely on the clip irrespective of stability.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Lung sliding is a sign, not a diagnosis. Correlate with clinical context and additional sonographic signs; artifacts and other conditions can mimic absent sliding.

practiceQuestions.stem: An IVC is plethoric in a patient with spontaneous breathing. Which statement best reflects evidence limits?

options.text: It proves adequate circulating volume.
It should be interpreted cautiously; IVC appearance depends on respiratory effort, ventilation and right-sided pressure, and should not alone dictate fluids.
It rules out obstructive shock.
A single IVC measurement determines fluid responsiveness.

practiceQuestions.rationale: IVC measures are context-sensitive; ACEP notes greater accuracy in mechanically ventilated settings and cautions that elevated right-sided pressures can produce a plethoric IVC.

practiceQuestions.stem: A scan is technically inadequate but no pathology is seen in acquired frames. Documentation?

options.text: Document negative examination.
Document limited/nondiagnostic study and why; obtain alternative expertise/imaging as clinical need dictates.
Delete the scan.
Report normal based on one view.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Absence of findings on incomplete images is not equivalent to a negative exam. Explicit limitation and next-step documentation supports safe integration and QA.

practiceQuestions.stem: A first-trimester patient has pain and no intrauterine pregnancy is visualized on a limited POCUS scan. Best conclusion?

options.text: Ectopic pregnancy confirmed.
Pregnancy location remains undetermined; clinical stability and follow-up/definitive evaluation are essential; absence of IUP alone is not diagnostic of ectopic pregnancy.
Pregnancy excluded.
No further evaluation needed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: An empty uterus in early pregnancy is not by itself proof of ectopic pregnancy; integrate symptoms, gestational timing, labs and follow-up/consultation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A vascular access attempt begins with a short-axis view. Which is the safety priority?

options.text: Advance whenever the needle disappears.
Maintain needle-tip visualization and sterile technique; stop/reposition if tip localization is lost.
Use only skin marking.
Ignore adjacent artery if vein compresses.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Dynamic real-time guidance requires tracking the tip, identifying adjacent anatomy, maintaining sterility and recognizing complications; educational viewing does not authorize unsupervised procedures.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which application classification reflects ACEP guidelines?

options.text: Emergency ultrasound is only radiology imaging.
Core emergency applications include trauma, pregnancy, cardiac/hemodynamic, aorta, thoracic/airway, biliary, urinary, DVT, soft tissue/MSK, ocular, bowel and procedural guidance.
Only FAST and cardiac are recognized.
Any ultrasound finding establishes final diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACEP identifies these 12 core applications and describes emergency POCUS as integrated diagnostic, resuscitative, monitoring and procedural work.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which credential statement is accurate as of 2026-10-07?

options.text: AEMUS is an ACGME-accredited board subspecialty.
ABEM offers an AEMUS Focused Practice Designation examination for eligible diplomates; EUFAC accredits AEMUS fellowships, not ACGME, and a fellowship or exam alone does not guarantee eligibility.
Every ultrasound fellowship graduate automatically receives FPD.
SCUF directory listing guarantees ABEM eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABEM labels AEMUS an FPD with eligibility/pathways; EUFAC states AEMUS fellowships are not ACGME-accredited and the ABEM FPD has additional eligibility criteria.

topicGaps: Verified free public viewing is 4.0092 hours (14,433 seconds) against the 36-hour video floor, leaving an actual 31.9908-hour gap; production targets, plans, readings and authored scripts are not counted as viewing hours.

The three newly counted recordings add 2.94 hours: a 54:56 ACS treatment-choice panel, a 56:34 ASMBS social-determinants/access webinar, and a 1:04:54 ASMBS ESG lecture. The first two are adjacent foundation content; only the latter is directly specialty procedural teaching.

No counted public lecture supplies a comprehensive current module on obesity pharmacotherapy, nutrition/deficiency management, anesthesia/airway planning, product-specific instructions for use, device-specific adverse-event treatment, TORe selection/follow-up, or a full altered-anatomy differential. The ASMBS 2016 nutrition guideline is a dated reading, not a current treatment protocol.

The candidate ASMBS 2025 ESG 2.0 recording had an observed 1:01:05 player duration but was flagged age-restricted by YouTube; accessible free viewing without age verification was not established and it is excluded. ASMBS BE-SAFE LMS modules are gated/login-based and excluded.

Public supply of freely accessible, substantive bariatric-endoscopy-specific lecture hours remains too limited to reach 36 hours without treating broad adjacent recordings as specialty content or inventing runtime. The residual hour gap is a real feasibility constraint, not a planned-production total.
The two inherited counted videos date from 2017 and 2021; all device status, recommendations and eligibility-related content must be checked against current primary sources.
No public evidence found for BWH didactic hour count, full rotations, ACGME accreditation of this named bariatric endoscopy fellowship, or a separate bariatric-endoscopy board exam.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: No separate ABIM/ABMS bariatric-endoscopy subspecialty board examination was identified in current ABIM exam/board listings checked 2026-10-07. ABIM Gastroenterology is the relevant underlying GI board exam; its January 2026 blueprint contains obesity management, procedures, and postsurgical bariatric topics. ABOM is a distinct obesity-medicine credential. ASMBS/SAGES describes BE-SAFE as an assessment-based certificate, explicitly not a formal professional certification. The BWH page recommends a path to ABOM for some trainees but does not imply automatic eligibility or certification.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: BWH’s public page states prerequisites of ABIM certification in Internal Medicine, projected successful completion of an ACGME-certified GI fellowship and GI board-eligibility, current clinical activity, and prior documented clinical research experience. These are BWH webpage statements, not independent verification of current selection rules; they are not board-eligibility guarantees. Verify all current rules with the program and ABIM/ABOM directly. This independent course grants no eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 42-year-old asks whether endoscopic bariatric therapy should be considered. Which statement best reflects the 2024 ASGE–ESGE guideline?

options.text: EBMT plus lifestyle modification is suggested for adults with BMI ≥30 kg/m², or BMI 27.0–29.9 kg/m² with at least one obesity-related comorbidity; this does not by itself establish individual candidacy.
EBMT is mandatory for anyone with BMI ≥27 kg/m².
EBMT replaces lifestyle treatment.
All EBMT devices have identical FDA indications.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The joint guideline conditionally suggests EBMT plus lifestyle modification in the stated BMI groups; shared decision-making, current device status, risk, and access remain essential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient asks whether the BWH Bariatric Endoscopy Fellowship creates eligibility for a separate bariatric endoscopy board examination. Best response?

options.text: Yes, completion alone grants a separate board credential.
No separate bariatric-endoscopy board examination is identified; ABIM Gastroenterology is an underlying certification pathway, while ABOM is a separate obesity-medicine credential.
The Fellowship Council administers the ABIM bariatric endoscopy exam.
ASMBS BE-SAFE is a state medical license.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The BWH page lists prior/anticipated GI training and mentions an ABOM path; ABIM lists Gastroenterology, not bariatric endoscopy, as its certification examination. BE-SAFE is an assessment-based certificate, not a formal professional certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner quotes a 2017 lecture for current gastric-balloon indications. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Accept it if the lecturer is a specialist.
Check current FDA device listings, device-specific labeling, and current society guidance; annotate the older lecture as historical.
Assume all balloons are available and interchangeable.
Use the video itself as an FDA label.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Device approvals and warnings change. FDA’s updated device page and product-specific current labeling, not an older lecture, should support current claims.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient reports severe persistent abdominal pain and repeated vomiting after a recent bariatric endoscopic procedure. Best educational response?

options.text: Reassure that nausea is expected and defer review.
Urgently assess and escalate through local emergency/procedural pathways for potential serious complication; do not diagnose remotely.
Recommend an unsupervised diet change only.
Wait until routine follow-up.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Persistent severe symptoms can signal a serious adverse event. The appropriate learning objective is urgent clinical evaluation/escalation, not remote diagnosis or management.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about ABIM GI blueprint alignment is accurate?

options.text: Bariatric endoscopy has its own ABIM content category.
Obesity management including medical, surgical, and endoscopic care appears under Nutrition 10.4; post-bariatric complications are also in gastric/duodenal disorders.
ABIM excludes procedures and periprocedural issues.
The whole GI exam is bariatric endoscopy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The January 2026 ABIM GI blueprint contains procedures/periprocedural issues, postsurgical gastric/duodenal conditions, and 10.4 obesity management within Nutrition.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fellow plans to reuse procedural video from a VideoGIE case in a course. Which approach respects rights?

options.text: Assume free access allows copying.
Link to the original publication/video; verify article-specific license and patient-consent/de-identification terms before any reuse.
Remove the author attribution and embed locally.
Use screenshots because still images are not protected.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public viewing is not a rehosting license. Source-linked viewing avoids copying; reuse requires checking specific rights and patient authorization/de-identification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient considering ESG has weight regain after prior bariatric surgery. Best first educational reasoning step?

options.text: Assume the same procedure is indicated.
Clarify prior anatomy, weight trajectory, symptoms, prior interventions, comorbidities, and patient goals with a multidisciplinary assessment before considering options.
Promise a specific weight-loss result.
Skip review of operative history.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical selection depends on altered anatomy, history, risks, goals and available alternatives; no outcome is guaranteed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes BE-SAFE?

options.text: It is a formal ABMS board certification.
It is an ASMBS/SAGES assessment-based certificate with video modules, written exam, and hands-on skills verification; the site says it is not a formal professional certification.
Its video course alone licenses an endoscopist.
It replaces case log and local privileges.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASMBS describes a fee-based assessment-based certificate and states explicitly that it is not a formal professional certification; procedural privilege decisions remain institution-specific.

practiceQuestions.stem: When discussing current FDA device status, which device class is specifically listed on the FDA page updated March 12, 2026?

options.text: Endoscopic suturing devices for altering gastric anatomy, linked to Apollo ESG and Revise Systems DEN210045.
Every investigational device from any country.
All experimental therapies as approved.
A single device class with permanent indication for any BMI.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The FDA current page lists endoscopic suturing devices for altering gastric anatomy and links to the DEN210045 De Novo decision; indication must be verified in the linked device document.

practiceQuestions.stem: A case vignette is being written for this self-study course. Which practice is acceptable?

options.text: Copy an identifiable patient chart because it is educational.
Create a clearly labeled fictional vignette, cite the clinical source, and avoid presenting it as a real patient.
Invent a case volume benchmark.
Claim the question predicts passing the ABIM exam.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Fictional educational cases are allowed if labeled; do not disclose patient records or make unsupported credentialing or prediction claims.

title: Advanced Endoscopy Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (post-Gastroenterology; this course is an independent, non-accredited self-study curriculum)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Intended level: physicians who have completed Gastroenterology fellowship (or equivalent advanced-GI foundation) and want cognitive preparation for advanced-endoscopy fellowship study; not a pre-med or technician course.
Working knowledge of diagnostic upper/lower endoscopy, GI anatomy, pancreaticobiliary disease, pathology, sedation/team safety and cross-sectional imaging.
Completion of a named institutional fellowship is not guaranteed; institution-specific eligibility, match, licensure and board requirements must be checked with the program/board.
This self-study cannot train or credential endoscope handling or any therapeutic procedure.
objectives: Frame an advanced endoscopic intervention as a clinical question with alternatives, expected decision impact and referral threshold.
Synthesize current ASGE/ESGE guidance for EUS tissue acquisition, ERCP, indeterminate biliary strictures, ESD and third-space procedures while preserving certainty/conditional qualifiers.
Distinguish diagnostic and therapeutic modalities, tissue diagnosis, drainage and staging; identify uncertainty and when multidisciplinary review is needed.
Recognize major adverse-event prevention, consent, escalation and quality-improvement principles.
Read authentic educational cases and media lawfully, with no copying of patient records/images and no unsupported procedural conclusions.
Use case-based reasoning in the broad ABIM Gastroenterology knowledge context without implying a separate advanced-endoscopy blueprint, credential, competence or passing prediction.

units.title: Scope, preparation, credentialing and safety
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: completed physician training in gastroenterology or equivalent advanced-GI foundation; basic diagnostic EGD/colonoscopy knowledge. Distinguish a cognitive learning track from accredited GME and procedural authorization.
objectives: Explain how BWH, Johns Hopkins and BIDMC describe distinct physician advanced-endoscopy fellowships and how duration/content vary by site.
Differentiate ABIM Gastroenterology certification from advanced-endoscopy training and the ASGE match.
Construct an indication/alternatives/consent/safety checklist that explicitly requires clinician judgment and local policy.
topics: Scope of a post-GI clinical fellowship; ASGE match versus board exam; accreditation limits; consent, sedation/team planning, anticoagulant and comorbidity risk; referral and escalation.
boardDomains: Gastroenterology scope / practice, prevention and counseling; certification eligibility and fellowship names are explicitly not ABIM domains.
units.casePractice: Case conference is for de-identified, lawfully hosted teaching resources or clearly labelled fictional educational vignettes. Learners must not copy/rehost patient records or images; see case access caveats.
units.assessment: Build an institutional-variant comparison and a patient-centered indication/alternatives matrix. Assessment: short-answer explanation plus safety checklist; no procedural skill rating.

units.title: Diagnostic EUS anatomy, lesion characterization and staging
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: Unit 1 and foundational cross-sectional imaging/anatomy; do not infer diagnosis from a single EUS feature.
objectives: Orient a linear echoendoscope view to relevant pancreaticobiliary landmarks using a structured sequence.
Describe a differential for a pancreatic, biliary, subepithelial or nodal finding and identify what additional context is needed.
Separate lesion detection, tissue diagnosis and staging questions, selecting complementary modalities conceptually.
topics: Linear EUS landmarks; transgastric/transduodenal views; Doppler safety concept; common artifacts; lesion characterization; staging questions; limitations and operator dependence.
boardDomains: ABIM GI cognitive practice: diagnostic reasoning and interpretation; no separately published advanced-endoscopy blueprint identified.
units.casePractice: Case conference is for de-identified, lawfully hosted teaching resources or clearly labelled fictional educational vignettes. Learners must not copy/rehost patient records or images; see case access caveats.
units.assessment: Make an annotated, source-linked landmark worksheet from the hosted Endoscopy Campus/EUS Club videos (no image exports); list three differentials and evidence gaps. Rubric: anatomy orientation 30%, differential/uncertainty 30%, modality logic 25%, citations/privacy 15%.

units.title: EUS-guided tissue acquisition and sample stewardship
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: Units 1–2; histology/cytology basics and the distinction between FNA and FNB.
objectives: Compare EUS-FNB and EUS-FNA evidence for a solid pancreatic mass using current ASGE recommendations and their GRADE strength.
Explain factors influencing needle choice and the roles of specimen handling, fanning, passes, rapid on-site evaluation and macroscopic evaluation.
Recognize how suspected lymphoma, metastatic disease, chronic pancreatitis, prior nondiagnostic sampling or planned therapy can change multidisciplinary planning.
topics: Indication versus incidental lesion; FNB/FNA evidence; vessel avoidance and visualization as conceptual safety checkpoints; tissue pathway; ROSE limits; specimen adequacy; second-review/escalation.
boardDomains: ABIM GI medical knowledge plus diagnostic clinical judgment; the ABIM blueprint is broader and not an advanced-endoscopy procedural exam.
units.casePractice: Case conference is for de-identified, lawfully hosted teaching resources or clearly labelled fictional educational vignettes. Learners must not copy/rehost patient records or images; see case access caveats.
units.assessment: Write a fictional multidisciplinary conference note comparing sampling strategies for two contrasting lesions; distinguish source facts from assumptions. Rubric: guideline use 35%, uncertainty/differential 25%, safety/sample plan 25%, communication 15%.

units.title: Biliary obstruction, ERCP indication and ductal tissue diagnosis
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: Units 1–3 and biliary anatomy/imaging; know when a less invasive diagnostic route is appropriate.
objectives: Classify the question ERCP is intended to answer and contrast its therapeutic versus diagnostic roles with EUS, MRCP and other pathways.
Apply the 2023 ASGE conditional framework for ERCP sampling/cholangioscopy and when additional EUS is suggested for undetermined biliary strictures.
Formulate a multidisciplinary information set including cross-sectional imaging, pathology, anatomy, drainage and patient priorities.
topics: Choledocholithiasis/obstruction; benign versus malignant stricture differential; brushing and fluoroscopy-guided biopsy; cholangioscopy context; EUS add-on indications; altered anatomy and referral.
boardDomains: ABIM GI diagnostic/treatment decision-making, biliary disease and complications; no board claim specific to advanced endoscopy.
units.casePractice: Case conference is for de-identified, lawfully hosted teaching resources or clearly labelled fictional educational vignettes. Learners must not copy/rehost patient records or images; see case access caveats.
units.assessment: Use a fictional indeterminate biliary-stricture case to create a decision tree comparing ERCP, EUS and noninvasive workup; cite evidence strength and alternatives. Rubric: indication logic 35%, correct qualifiers 30%, safety/drainage 20%, citations 15%.

units.title: ERCP cognitive sequence, cannulation risk and pancreatitis prevention
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: Units 1, 3–4; this is cognitive review, not hands-on cannulation training.
objectives: Summarize the relative evidence for rectal NSAIDs, wire-guided cannulation, prophylactic pancreatic stents and hydration in the ASGE PEP-prevention guideline.
Recognize and state guideline qualifiers/contraindications rather than turn population recommendations into a patient-specific order.
Analyze a fictional escalation scenario after difficult cannulation and identify which information must be communicated to the attending/team.
topics: Procedure intent; papillary/duct anatomy; access attempts as a risk signal; PEP prevention; cholangitis, bleeding, perforation and sedation events; postprocedure monitoring and escalation.
boardDomains: ABIM GI evidence-based decision-making, adverse-event recognition and safety; exact detailed skills/procedure assessment remains institutional.
units.casePractice: Case conference is for de-identified, lawfully hosted teaching resources or clearly labelled fictional educational vignettes. Learners must not copy/rehost patient records or images; see case access caveats.
units.assessment: Submit a one-page event-analysis/mitigation map for fictional high-risk ERCP scenarios. Rubric: correct prevention evidence 40%, contraindication/context qualifiers 25%, escalation/monitoring 25%, readability 10%.

units.title: Pancreatic cysts, chronic pancreatitis and fluid collections
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: Units 2–5 and pancreatic disease fundamentals; distinguish a cystic lesion from acute/chronic inflammatory collection.
objectives: Construct a differential for pancreatic cystic lesions and distinguish the role/limits of EUS characterization and tissue/fluid analysis.
Identify management questions that require current guideline review, multidisciplinary planning and longitudinal imaging rather than an isolated image impression.
Compare conceptual indications and safety issues for EUS-guided drainage of pancreatic fluid collections, including collection maturity/contents and anatomy.
topics: Cystic neoplasm risk features; EUS sampling trade-offs; chronic pancreatitis pain/ductal disease; pseudocyst vs walled-off necrosis; drainage access and adverse-event domains; endoscopic necrosectomy referral.
boardDomains: ABIM GI pancreatic disease differential, risk assessment and longitudinal follow-up; no volumes or outcomes inferred.
units.casePractice: Case conference is for de-identified, lawfully hosted teaching resources or clearly labelled fictional educational vignettes. Learners must not copy/rehost patient records or images; see case access caveats.
units.assessment: Compare one source-hosted EUS cyst lecture and one source-hosted fluid-collection case by evidence question, not by copied image. Rubric: differential 30%, cyst/collection distinction 25%, indication/alternatives 25%, currentness/privacy 20%.

units.title: EMR/ESD, endoscopic resection and pathology-based decisions
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: Units 1–2 and neoplasia/pathology principles; formal supervised technical training is outside this course.
objectives: Distinguish lesion assessment and referral decisions for snare-based EMR versus en-bloc ESD without claiming eligibility from image alone.
Interpret the 2022 ESGE guideline's limits on routine pre-resection EUS/cross-sectional imaging and on ESD selection by site/feature.
Translate margin, depth, differentiation, lymphovascular invasion and other histology into a need for staging/MDT review versus endoscopic follow-up, preserving the guideline's qualifiers.
topics: High-definition/chromoendoscopic characterization; lesion morphology and fibrosis; en-bloc/piecemeal trade-offs; specimen orientation; curative/local-risk/high-risk categories; surveillance and surgical discussion.
boardDomains: ABIM GI neoplasia, interpretation, treatment selection and follow-up; the detailed ESD guideline is an external evidence supplement, not an ABIM AEF blueprint.
units.casePractice: Case conference is for de-identified, lawfully hosted teaching resources or clearly labelled fictional educational vignettes. Learners must not copy/rehost patient records or images; see case access caveats.
units.assessment: Create a pathology-linked resection conference worksheet from the CC-BY E-Videos article through its source page; use text descriptions/links only, not copied patient images. Rubric: lesion/resection rationale 30%, histology risk stratification 35%, alternative/MDT reasoning 20%, rights/source citation 15%.

units.title: Third-space endoscopy and motility interventions
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: Units 1–2 and esophageal/gastric motility principles.
objectives: Explain conceptual differences among POEM, G-POEM, Z-POEM and ESD/STER without treating them as interchangeable procedures.
Identify the diagnostic confirmation, patient selection, alternative therapies, multidisciplinary and outcome questions to resolve before an intervention.
Analyze source lecture and case outcomes while accounting for limited follow-up and single-center/video-case publication bias.
topics: Achalasia phenotypes and therapy choice; tunneling/myotomy concepts; G-POEM evidence/indications and evolving evidence; Z-POEM/septotomy; reflux/other adverse events; shared decision-making.
boardDomains: ABIM GI motility and decision-making; no procedural competence or success claim.
units.casePractice: Case conference is for de-identified, lawfully hosted teaching resources or clearly labelled fictional educational vignettes. Learners must not copy/rehost patient records or images; see case access caveats.
units.assessment: Prepare an evidence appraisal of the G-POEM lecture and the linked Z-POEM teaching case, separating technique observation from comparative efficacy. Rubric: indication/alternatives 30%, evidence appraisal 35%, safety/follow-up 20%, source/rights discipline 15%.

units.title: Luminal therapy, Barrett's neoplasia and bariatric/antireflux methods
objectives: Compare the cognitive purposes and limitations of Barrett's resection/ablation, luminal stenting, TIF and endoscopic bariatric therapies.
State how referral, multidisciplinary planning, patient goals and guideline currency influence choosing among endoscopic, medical and surgical pathways.
Identify harms, technical failure, recurrence and surveillance questions requiring longitudinal evidence.
topics: Barrett's dysplasia and visible lesion strategy; ablation following appropriate assessment; strictures/obstruction and stent trade-offs; endoscopic bariatric interventions; TIF; case selection and follow-up.
boardDomains: ABIM GI esophageal disease, neoplasia and treatment selection. The treatment pathways are not instructions to perform or certify a procedure.

units.assessment: Write a comparative shared-decision memo for a fictional Barrett/foregut scenario; list guideline version date and alternative care. Rubric: accurate scope 30%, alternatives/risks 30%, follow-up 25%, source/date 15%.

units.title: Deep enteroscopy, complex anatomy and therapeutic rescue
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: Units 1, 4–6; awareness of altered anatomy and small-bowel bleeding/obstruction.
objectives: Describe where enteroscopy, capsule endoscopy, ERCP and EUS answer different clinical questions in altered anatomy or obscure bleeding.
Recognize the special anatomic, infection, drainage and adverse-event constraints for complex ERCP/EUS and when to refer to a center of expertise.
Outline an escalation/rescue handoff, including anatomic history, imaging, prior interventions and multidisciplinary roles.
topics: Single/deep enteroscopy; altered post-surgical anatomy; EUS-guided drainage/ERCP rescue; foreign body/stent; bleeding; perforation, infection and adverse events; surgical/IR collaboration.
boardDomains: ABIM GI small-bowel, biliary, bleeding and safety reasoning; complex technical skills require supervised program training.
units.casePractice: Case conference is for de-identified, lawfully hosted teaching resources or clearly labelled fictional educational vignettes. Learners must not copy/rehost patient records or images; see case access caveats.
units.assessment: Construct an altered-anatomy handoff map from a hypothetical case; identify the procedural questions reserved for an expert. Rubric: anatomy/history 30%, modality/referral reasoning 30%, adverse events/escalation 25%, communication 15%.

units.title: Quality, consent, complications, research and responsible learning
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: all previous units; complete this before integrated case conference.
objectives: Use explicit denominators, outcomes and limitations when interpreting published advanced-endoscopy evidence; avoid unverified volume or success thresholds.
Design a small process audit with a defined question, de-identified/non-patient-level aggregate measures, and a balancing measure.
Identify consent, conflicts, access, reproducibility, disclosure and follow-up issues in educational videos, device-sponsored material and case reports.
topics: Evidence appraisal; adverse-event systems; consent, documentation, team communication, QI, prospective trials, study design, learning curves, privileging and source rights.
boardDomains: ABIM professionalism, practice-based learning, quality and systems-based reasoning. No observed procedural entrustment assessment.

units.assessment: Submit a 1-page QI proposal and source/license checklist; do not use patient-level data. Rubric: measure/question 30%, bias/limitations 25%, privacy/consent 25%, feasibility/citations 20%.

units.title: Integrated board-cognitive case conference and longitudinal plan
units.prerequisites: Prerequisite: Units 1–11; scenario questions assess reasoning only.
objectives: Synthesize symptoms, imaging, pathology, anatomy, patient priorities and guideline strength to justify a next diagnostic/therapeutic question rather than an automatic procedure.
Discuss at least one plausible alternative and a contingency/escalation route for EUS, ERCP, resection and third-space cases.
Explain how follow-up, pathology review, adverse-event review, institutional expertise and evidence date alter the plan.
topics: Pancreatic solid mass; indeterminate biliary stricture; resection specimen; motility/third-space choice; competing modalities; guideline qualifiers; reflection and review schedule.
boardDomains: Maps to broad ABIM GI knowledge and higher-order case judgment, not to a separate advanced-endoscopy exam, validated readiness prediction or competency sign-off.

assignment.title: Advanced Endoscopy Cognitive Portfolio
deliverables: Two modality-selection memos (one pancreaticobiliary and one luminal/third-space); state question, alternatives, guideline date, evidence strength and referral/escalation point.

One evidence appraisal comparing a current guideline recommendation and a source-hosted lecture/case; identify uncertainty, conflicts, publication date and what is not established.

unitMap.text: Scope, preparation, credentialing and safety
coveredTopics: Scope of a post-GI clinical fellowship; ASGE match versus board exam; accreditation limits; consent, sedation/team planning, anticoagulant and comorbidity risk; referral and escalation.

unitMap.text: Diagnostic EUS anatomy, lesion characterization and staging
coveredTopics: Linear EUS landmarks; transgastric/transduodenal views; Doppler safety concept; common artifacts; lesion characterization; staging questions; limitations and operator dependence.

unitMap.text: EUS-guided tissue acquisition and sample stewardship
coveredTopics: Indication versus incidental lesion; FNB/FNA evidence; vessel avoidance and visualization as conceptual safety checkpoints; tissue pathway; ROSE limits; specimen adequacy; second-review/escalation.

unitMap.text: Biliary obstruction, ERCP indication and ductal tissue diagnosis
coveredTopics: Choledocholithiasis/obstruction; benign versus malignant stricture differential; brushing and fluoroscopy-guided biopsy; cholangioscopy context; EUS add-on indications; altered anatomy and referral.

unitMap.text: ERCP cognitive sequence, cannulation risk and pancreatitis prevention
coveredTopics: Procedure intent; papillary/duct anatomy; access attempts as a risk signal; PEP prevention; cholangitis, bleeding, perforation and sedation events; postprocedure monitoring and escalation.

unitMap.text: Pancreatic cysts, chronic pancreatitis and fluid collections
coveredTopics: Cystic neoplasm risk features; EUS sampling trade-offs; chronic pancreatitis pain/ductal disease; pseudocyst vs walled-off necrosis; drainage access and adverse-event domains; endoscopic necrosectomy referral.

unitMap.text: EMR/ESD, endoscopic resection and pathology-based decisions
coveredTopics: High-definition/chromoendoscopic characterization; lesion morphology and fibrosis; en-bloc/piecemeal trade-offs; specimen orientation; curative/local-risk/high-risk categories; surveillance and surgical discussion.

unitMap.text: Third-space endoscopy and motility interventions
coveredTopics: Achalasia phenotypes and therapy choice; tunneling/myotomy concepts; G-POEM evidence/indications and evolving evidence; Z-POEM/septotomy; reflux/other adverse events; shared decision-making.

unitMap.text: Luminal therapy, Barrett's neoplasia and bariatric/antireflux methods
coveredTopics: Barrett's dysplasia and visible lesion strategy; ablation following appropriate assessment; strictures/obstruction and stent trade-offs; endoscopic bariatric interventions; TIF; case selection and follow-up.

unitMap.text: Deep enteroscopy, complex anatomy and therapeutic rescue
coveredTopics: Single/deep enteroscopy; altered post-surgical anatomy; EUS-guided drainage/ERCP rescue; foreign body/stent; bleeding; perforation, infection and adverse events; surgical/IR collaboration.

unitMap.text: Quality, consent, complications, research and responsible learning
coveredTopics: Evidence appraisal; adverse-event systems; consent, documentation, team communication, QI, prospective trials, study design, learning curves, privileging and source rights.

unitMap.text: Integrated board-cognitive case conference and longitudinal plan
coveredTopics: Pancreatic solid mass; indeterminate biliary stricture; resection specimen; motility/third-space choice; competing modalities; guideline qualifiers; reflection and review schedule.

topicGaps: Verified specialty-specific public full lecture media totals 27,394 seconds / 7.609444 hours after this expansion, leaving a residual 102,206 seconds / 28.390556 hours against the 36-hour specialty-specific target. Only actual free-to-view verified external recording durations count; targets, script estimates, reading, case-study and planned-film minutes are excluded.

The newly verified recordings materially expand systematic EUS examination, pancreatobiliary/liver/gallbladder/mediastinal anatomy, pancreatic solid and cystic lesions, biopsy-negative/submucosal lesions, and small-bowel therapy. Coverage remains uneven and the ESGE webinar is not a complete small-bowel fellowship curriculum.

No counted full-length specialty recording was verified for difficult ERCP cannulation practice, complete ERCP adverse-event rescue, therapeutic-EUS drainage, Barrett eradication, biliary strictures specifically, altered-anatomy ERCP, live supervised ESD or human procedure assessment; original written episodes address selected cognitive gaps but do not count as recordings or replace clinical teaching.

No public complete institutional didactic set, separate advanced-endoscopy ABIM blueprint, AEF board examination, case-volume requirement, or supervised procedural competency evaluation was verified. Institutional teaching may exist privately/restricted; user-requested access restrictions precluded paywall or login bypass.

Several source-hosted case demonstrations remain runtime-unverified, do not establish general licensing/de-identification, and contribute zero hours; link-only case use and original fictional cases are retained.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.
