medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (post-Gastroenterology; this course is an independent, non-accredited self-study curriculum)
boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) Gastroenterology Certification Examination
medical.boardStatus: No separate Advanced Endoscopy board examination or ABIM certificate was identified in the current ABIM examination/certification sources reviewed. ABIM Gastroenterology certification is a separate, formal subspecialty process requiring ABIM Internal Medicine certification, requisite accredited Gastroenterology fellowship training, clinical competence and the ABIM GI examination. ASGE's Advanced Endoscopy Fellowship Match is a selection match, not a board examination. This research does not rule out every non-ABIM certificate or jurisdiction-specific credential.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This course does not establish eligibility for any board. Verify requirements with ABIM and the relevant regulator. ABIM Gastroenterology certification requirements include prior Internal Medicine certification and required accredited Gastroenterology fellowship training; this independent program is not credit toward either requirement.

officialProgrammes.institution: Brigham and Women's Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: BWH Advanced Endoscopy Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official BWH page describes a clinical therapeutic endoscopy fellowship. Exposure includes ERCP; diagnostic/therapeutic EUS; EMR/ESD; deep enteroscopy; Barrett's ablation; confocal endomicroscopy; third-space POEM/G-POEM/Z-POEM; TIF; and bariatric methods. It describes one-on-one work with faculty and research/clinical trials. Page states academic GI fellowship completion within five years is required, with research/academic-career preferences. It does not publish a complete didactic video set, formal ACGME AEF accreditation or duration of an AEF board exam.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins Hospital / Johns Hopkins Medicine
officialProgrammes.name: Advanced Endoscopy Fellowship Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a two-year clinical fellowship geared to academic endoscopy, a pancreaticobiliary core with ERCP/EUS, EMR, stenting, ablation and enteroscopy; selected second-year advanced procedures; didactics, clinics, conferences, inpatient service and research. It participates in the ASGE AEF match. No public exact rotation ledger or separate AEF board credential was found.

officialProgrammes.institution: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC; Harvard Medical School teaching hospital)
officialProgrammes.name: Advanced Endoscopy
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official GI/Medicine GME fellowship page describes mostly one-year training, ERCP (including altered anatomy/cholangioscopy), diagnostic/interventional EUS, EMR, luminal work and emerging techniques; its application page requires prior three-year ACGME-accredited GI fellowship or at least three years GI education for non-ACGME graduates. There is conflicting public wording: the fellowship page says two ASGE-matched slots plus another sponsored opportunity; its application page says three clinical fellowship positions via ASGE match. Verify current slots directly; this record preserves, not resolves, the discrepancy.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The saved MED-X029 discovery packet identified BWH. Follow-up primary-source verification identified distinct official Hopkins and BIDMC advanced-endoscopy clinical physician fellowship offerings and preserves their exact institutional names. These are institution-specific variants within one specialty course, not a combined programme or shared curriculum. BIDMC explicitly calls its page a fellowship within the GI/Medicine GME program; Hopkins has a dedicated advanced-endoscopy fellowship page. BWH, Hopkins and BIDMC are clinical physician training rather than non-physician technician categories. BWH/Hopkins describe research as integrated with clinical training; no separate research-only advanced endoscopy postdoctoral track was verified. MGH general GI page was not treated as an additional AEF. This scoped review is not proof that no other Harvard-affiliated offer exists; an accessible separate AEF page was verified only at the institutions named above.
sourceCaveats: Public webpages describe the content the institutions choose to publish, not a complete official curriculum, live faculty lectures, case volumes, rotations or competency results.

ACGME's 2025 requirement is for the 36-month Gastroenterology fellowship; the review did not verify separate ACGME accreditation for the institution-specific Advanced Endoscopy fellowships. Absence of such text on a page is not a definitive accreditation search result.

ABIM's official GI page lists its Gastroenterology exam, but no separate Advanced Endoscopy exam/certificate appeared in the ABIM list checked. The course does not claim universal absence of other professional certificates.
ASGE AEF participation/matching is not equivalent to ACGME accreditation, licensure or ABIM board eligibility.
BIDMC public pages conflict on the number and match status of available clinical positions; confirm directly with program leadership.
A patient-level medical literature case or open clinical video is not permission to copy/rehost an image or clinical record; course case work uses source links only.
Clinical and board status checked 2026-10-07. Guidance may change; recheck the cited board and guidelines before clinical use.

Medical human review was not performed; independent education has no Harvard/JHU/BIDMC/ASGE/ACGME affiliation, accreditation, training credit, clinical licensure, board eligibility, procedural competence, certification, or guaranteed passing.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional educational case: the team has decided that tissue is needed from an EUS-accessible solid pancreatic mass. Under the current ASGE recommendation, which needle class is preferred?

options.text: FNA in every case because cytology is always superior
FNB over FNA
No sampling is ever appropriate
Choose a needle solely from lesion size

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASGE strongly recommends FNB rather than FNA for EUS tissue acquisition from a solid pancreatic mass; the recommendation is moderate-certainty, not a guarantee for an individual case. The indication, alternative routes and patient-specific risks still require the treating team.

practiceQuestions.stem: For EUS tissue acquisition in a solid pancreatic mass, what does the ASGE guideline say about needle gauge?

options.text: It suggests 22-gauge over 25-gauge, with a conditional recommendation; switch/consider another gauge when manipulability or access is problematic
It strongly prohibits 25-gauge needles
Gauge has no role in the choice
Always use the largest available gauge

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 22-gauge preference over 25-gauge is conditional, not absolute. The guideline notes that a 25-gauge needle can be considered when a 22-gauge needle is difficult to advance or has limited maneuverability.
practiceQuestions.domain: Guideline strength and EUS tissue acquisition

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner asks whether rapid on-site cytopathology evaluation (ROSE) is mandatory for every EUS sample of a solid pancreatic mass. Which answer best matches the ASGE guideline?

options.text: Yes, always and regardless of context
No; ASGE suggests against routine ROSE, while listing situations in which it may be considered
ROSE replaces histopathology
ROSE is required only for a 25-gauge needle

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASGE suggests against routine ROSE for these cases (conditional, low-quality evidence) and describes contexts such as a prior nondiagnostic sample or an obscured/uncertain lesion where it may be considered. This is not a universal rule for all EUS indications.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult without a contraindication is scheduled for ERCP. Which preventive measure is recommended by the ASGE PEP-prevention guideline for unselected adults?

options.text: Preprocedural rectal NSAID; screen for relevant contraindications and use clinical judgment
Antibiotics in every patient
Avoid all preventive measures unless pancreatitis occurs
Routine prophylactic pancreatic stenting in every patient

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ASGE guideline recommends preprocedural rectal NSAIDs in unselected patients as well as high-risk patients, with qualifiers including avoidance in recent peptic ulcer disease or renal insufficiency. This question tests a guideline principle, not an individual order or dosing instruction.

practiceQuestions.stem: In unselected patients undergoing ERCP, what cannulation approach does the ASGE PEP guideline suggest to reduce post-ERCP pancreatitis risk?

options.text: Wire-guided cannulation over contrast-guided cannulation
Repeated forceful pancreatic duct wire advancement
Routine pancreatic duct contrast injection before every attempt
No attempt to limit duct trauma

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASGE conditionally suggests wire-guided over contrast-guided cannulation. It also emphasizes avoiding forceful or repeated wire advancement into the pancreatic duct. The course does not teach or authorize hands-on cannulation.
practiceQuestions.domain: ERCP adverse-event prevention and procedural reasoning

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient is categorized by the treating endoscopist as high-risk for post-ERCP pancreatitis and the pancreatic duct has been repeatedly or deeply accessed. Which preventive action is supported by the ASGE guideline?

options.text: Use a prophylactic pancreatic stent in high-risk patients with repeated/deep pancreatic duct access, when clinically appropriate
Place a biliary stent solely to prevent pancreatitis
No prevention is possible
Always add a sphincterotomy regardless of indication

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASGE recommends pancreatic stents in high-risk patients in whom the pancreatic duct has been repeatedly or deeply accessed, and conditionally suggests one when access is readily achievable in high-risk patients. The decision is for trained clinicians using patient-specific context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has a biliary stricture of undetermined cause and is undergoing ERCP. Which sampling plan matches the ASGE 2023 recommendation?

options.text: ASGE suggests adding fluoroscopy-guided biopsy to brush cytology rather than brush cytology alone; this is conditional and based on very-low-quality evidence
Brush cytology alone is the only acceptable method
Cholangioscopy is mandatory in every stricture regardless of expertise or drainage
A sample makes multidisciplinary review unnecessary

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASGE conditionally suggests adding fluoroscopy-guided biopsy sampling to brush cytology. Evidence certainty is very low; cross-sectional imaging review, drainage considerations, available expertise and multidisciplinary interpretation remain important.
practiceQuestions.domain: Biliary stricture work-up and evidence strength

practiceQuestions.stem: For an undetermined biliary stricture, in which setting does ASGE suggest cholangioscopy-guided biopsy may be considered?

options.text: Selected nondistal strictures with a high probability of adequate drainage, prior nondiagnostic ERCP without cholangioscopy, and a center with expertise/equipment
Every stricture before any imaging review
Only where drainage of the relevant segment is impossible
As a substitute for all histopathology

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2023 ASGE recommendation is conditional and restricted to selected contexts, including nondistal strictures when adequate drainage is likely, a prior nondiagnostic ERCP, and local clinical expertise/equipment. Irrigation and drainage risks matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has a distal biliary stricture and an initial ERCP sample was nondiagnostic. According to ASGE's undetermined-stricture guideline, what additional modality should be considered?

options.text: EUS in addition to ERCP for diagnosis, particularly in specified settings such as a distal stricture or prior nondiagnostic ERCP
Repeat identical ERCPs indefinitely without reassessment
Do not review cross-sectional imaging
Assume a benign stricture without follow-up

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASGE suggests EUS in addition to ERCP for a distal stricture, prior nondiagnostic ERCP, or imaging evidence of lymphadenopathy/metastatic disease, while noting very-low-quality evidence and the need for context. Hilar-stricture sampling has specific cautionary issues.

practiceQuestions.stem: Before resection of a superficial GI lesion, which statement reflects the 2022 ESGE ESD guideline?

options.text: Routine EUS, CT, MRI or PET-CT is not recommended before endoscopic resection of superficial lesions; selection is based on expert endoscopic assessment and relevant context
All superficial lesions require routine PET-CT and EUS
Histology never changes management
ESD is routine for every duodenal lesion

practiceQuestions.rationale: ESGE recommends expert evaluation using high-definition white light and chromoendoscopy and does not recommend routine EUS/CT/MRI/PET-CT before endoscopic resection. ESD suitability varies by site and features; pathology and high-risk findings can trigger staging and multidisciplinary treatment discussion.
practiceQuestions.domain: Resection selection, staging and evidence interpretation

assignment.description: Using an original hypothetical vignette, create a time-anchored episode map; list candidate diagnoses and competing explanations; identify missing information and consent-aware collateral; complete a safety-domain checklist and escalation triggers; compare relevant recommendations from one current guideline and one alternate jurisdiction; state what must be referred to a licensed clinician. Risk and escalation checklist
Evidence table naming source/date/population/limitations
Five-minute oral handoff using non-stigmatizing language

unitMap.text: Episode classification and DSM-aligned bipolar spectrum
coveredTopics: Differentiate bipolar I, bipolar II, cyclothymic, substance/medication-induced, due-to-medical-condition, other specified, and unspecified categories using longitudinal episode features.
Explain why a bipolar I diagnosis requires mania while bipolar II requires both hypomania and major depression.
Distinguish mania, hypomania, major depressive episodes, mixed features, and rapid cycling without treating screening scores as diagnoses.

unitMap.text: Longitudinal formulation and differential diagnosis
coveredTopics: Build a timeline of mood/energy/sleep/function changes using patient account, collateral, records with consent, and prospective tracking.
Compare episodic mania/hypomania with unipolar depression, ADHD, trauma-related symptoms, borderline personality patterns, psychotic disorders, substances/medications, and medical mimics.
State how a positive screen changes the need for assessment but does not establish diagnosis.

unitMap.text: Assessment, risk, and level-of-care reasoning
coveredTopics: Conduct a structured psychiatric history and mental-status assessment, including psychosis, sleep, functioning, substance use, medications, medical comorbidity, prior response and adverse effects.
Assess suicide/self-harm, violence, self-neglect, exploitation, financial/sexual disinhibition, ability to care for self, and protective factors.
Identify findings that require urgent in-person emergency/specialist assessment rather than self-study or outpatient reassurance.

unitMap.text: Acute mania, hypomania, psychosis, and mixed features
coveredTopics: Prioritize safety, setting, sleep/substance factors, medication reconciliation, and treatment response in an acute manic presentation.
Summarize guideline-supported acute mania options and sequencing at a principle level without prescribing an individualized regimen.
Recognize when psychosis, severe impairment, inability to care for self, or risk requires urgent specialist/emergency care.

unitMap.text: Bipolar depression and antidepressant-related complexity
coveredTopics: Identify depressive episodes in bipolar illness and features prompting a careful history for prior hypomania/mania.
Compare evidence frameworks for acute bipolar depression and discuss caution around antidepressant monotherapy and treatment-emergent affective switch.
Include suicide risk, preference, prior response, mixed symptoms, and comorbidities in a conceptual treatment plan.

unitMap.text: Maintenance, relapse prevention, and recovery
coveredTopics: Explain why bipolar care is longitudinal and collaborative, with acute stabilization, recovery goals, relapse prevention, and repeated review.
Design a fictional early-warning/relapse-prevention plan involving sleep/rhythm, adherence barriers, support people with consent, and crisis contacts.
Discuss monitoring and functional outcomes without assuming one intervention works for everyone.

unitMap.text: Psychopharmacology, safety monitoring, and interactions
coveredTopics: Compare major medication classes used in guideline pathways at the level of phase evidence, common safety issues, interactions, and monitoring principles.
Identify the need to check renal/thyroid/metabolic status and drug interactions where indicated by treatment and guidelines.
Explain why medication initiation, dose changes, stopping, and monitoring require a licensed prescriber and individualized assessment.

unitMap.text: Psychotherapy, psychoeducation, and social rhythm interventions
coveredTopics: Describe guideline-supported adjunctive psychosocial approaches, including psychoeducation and structured psychotherapy, at a conceptual level.
Explain how interpersonal/social rhythm, sleep regularity, family involvement with consent, and self-management may support relapse prevention.
Critically separate adjunctive supports from urgent assessment or indicated medical treatment.

unitMap.text: Youth, development, and transition of care
coveredTopics: Apply developmentally informed assessment, collateral from caregivers when appropriate, school/social functioning, consent/capacity, and safeguarding considerations.
Differentiate episodic mania/hypomania from chronic irritability and overlapping neurodevelopmental presentations using validated diagnostic criteria and specialist assessment.
Avoid diagnosing from family history, irritability, or a screening scale alone; note jurisdiction-specific guideline differences.

unitMap.text: Pregnancy, postpartum, and reproductive safety
coveredTopics: Recognize that pregnancy planning, pregnancy, postpartum, lactation, and paternal exposure alter risk-benefit discussions and require current specialist guidance.
Identify serious valproate reproductive-risk protections and distinguish the UK MHRA framework from other jurisdictions and FDA labeling.
Use shared decision-making and avoid abrupt discontinuation or medication changes without clinical advice.

unitMap.text: Older adults, comorbidity, and integrated care
coveredTopics: Consider medical, neurologic, cognitive, substance-use, anxiety, and sleep comorbidity in a differential and treatment-safety review.
Adapt assessment for later-life changes, polypharmacy, cognition, sensory access, and medical causes without assuming new symptoms are bipolar illness.
Plan integrated collaboration and continuity rather than fragmenting co-occurring conditions.

unitMap.text: Evidence appraisal, ethics, and quality improvement
coveredTopics: Map a focused question to the current ABPN blueprint and compare guideline scope, dates, evidence certainty, and population.
Identify conflicts of interest, trial limitations, external validity, access inequities, and when local law/product labeling differs.
Propose a measurable educational/quality-improvement aim without claiming a clinical outcome or board-passing result.

topicGaps: One additional official public mood-dynamics grand-rounds recording (1:02:40) is counted as foundation, not bipolar-specific teaching. The observed accessible ledger is 2.391067 hours (8607.84 seconds) versus the 36-hour target; the residual gap is 33.608933 hours.

No verified full-length recordings were located for structured bipolar diagnostic interviewing/differential practice, mania safety and guideline comparison, adult bipolar depression treatment decision-making, pharmacology monitoring and reproductive counseling, psychotherapy/maintenance, youth assessment, or ethics/quality improvement. The public UT Health San Antonio youth lecture has only an approximate spoken runtime; Silver Hill late-life bipolar and UMB/other YouTube candidates lacked independently confirmed exact player runtime during this check and remain uncounted.

The 36 planned source-backed clip plans are production targets only, not actual videos or rendered hours. Original authored episodes are scripts only; no media rendering, runtime probe, qualified human clinical review or rights clearance has occurred. External production would need to create, independently review, render, rights-clear, host accessibly and probe a very large residual duration before any portion could be credited.

officialProgrammes.institution: McLean Hospital (Mass General Brigham; Harvard Medical School affiliate)
officialProgrammes.name: Frazier Research Institute and the Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder Program Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official postgraduate-fellowships page places this entry under Research Fellowships, not the Clinical Fellowships list. It describes two years of funding for research on psychotic disorders; psychiatrists in PGY-4 or within one year after residency may apply. Training is mainly participation in research with senior-faculty teaching/supervision and opportunities to participate in clinical care for bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and related conditions. It mentions clinical, neuroimaging, genetic and preclinical research, research ethics, grant writing, publications and expectation of external funding applications. The page does not publish a bipolar clinical rotation curriculum, formal case minimums, accreditation status, selection guarantee, or bipolar-specific board eligibility.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet title “Bipolar Disorders Fellowship” is retained as the course title, but the institution’s own directory heading is “Frazier Research Institute and the Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder Program Fellowship.” The official page classifies it under research fellowships. It is a psychiatrist-targeted research fellowship with some clinical-care opportunities, not substantiated as a dedicated clinical bipolar-disorders fellowship or ACGME-accredited bipolar subspecialty. It is not a combined psychiatry residency or a non-physician training track. No institutional rotations are published in the source reviewed; this curriculum does not invent them. ACGME’s psychiatry page lists program requirements and recognized subspecialty programs; ABPN’s current certification page lists psychiatry subspecialty exams but not bipolar disorders. No bipolar-specific board exam was identified.
sourceCaveats: No human clinical review was performed. Verify each clinical claim, medication safety issue, label and guideline before clinical use.

NICE/MHRA is UK guidance; VA/DoD and ABPN apply to specific U.S. contexts; CANMAT/ISBD is an international evidence framework. Their recommendations, approval status, age scope and legal rules are not interchangeable.
The institution’s public description is not a complete syllabus and does not establish ACGME accreditation, appointment, clinical workload, individual eligibility, outcomes or case volume.

Search/discovery and webpage/transcript metadata are not substitutes for formal licensing/access verification; uncounted videos stay uncounted until exact duration and unrestricted free access are confirmed.
Authentic published case resources are links only. No patient records, case text or diagnostic images have been copied. Copyright, consent and access limitations vary by item.
Fictional cases/questions and self-study do not authorize treatment or procedure; no passing, diagnosis, credential, licensure or competence is guaranteed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person has had one clearly documented manic episode requiring hospitalization and no prior major depressive episode. Which diagnostic principle is most accurate?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder requires a history of major depression.
A manic episode can meet the defining episode requirement for bipolar I even without prior major depression.
The history supports bipolar II because hospitalization defines hypomania.
A positive mood screening questionnaire alone is sufficient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Bipolar I is distinguished by at least one manic episode; major depression is not required. Diagnosis still depends on full criteria, context, and exclusion of causes.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABPN Dimension 1: bipolar and related disorders; diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has recurrent depression. A screening instrument is positive for bipolar-spectrum symptoms, but the patient recalls no clear elevated episodes. What is the best next conceptual step?

options.text: Diagnose bipolar II based on the screen.
Start an antidepressant immediately without further history.
Obtain a detailed longitudinal mood/energy history, collateral if available/consented, substance/medication review, and consider prospective tracking.
Exclude bipolar disorder because the patient sought care during depression.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening instruments can flag the need for further evaluation but are not diagnostic. Longitudinal history, collateral where appropriate, and prospective monitoring can clarify episodicity.
practiceQuestions.domain: CANMAT/ISBD diagnostic assessment; ABPN diagnostic procedures.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which feature most strongly distinguishes an episodic manic syndrome from chronic irritability alone in a young person?

options.text: Family history alone.
Abrupt episodic change in mood with increased energy/activity and a distinct time course, interpreted by a qualified clinician.
A single angry outburst.
School difficulty without a change from baseline.

practiceQuestions.rationale: An episodic change in mood/energy and longitudinal course matter. Irritability is nonspecific, and youth diagnosis needs developmental assessment and guideline-specific care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient presents with severe activation, psychotic symptoms, minimal sleep, and inability to safely care for self. What is the priority?

options.text: Routine self-guided online follow-up.
Urgent in-person emergency/specialist assessment and immediate safety planning.
Wait several months for mood charting.
Use a screening scale to determine outpatient medication choice.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Severe impairment, psychosis, and compromised self-care require urgent clinical assessment; educational material cannot substitute for emergency care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician re-evaluates a depressive presentation after a history of possible activation emerges. Which statement is safest?

options.text: Antidepressant monotherapy is always safe in possible bipolar illness.
Clarify diagnosis, mixed symptoms, risk, past treatment response, and specialist guidance before making treatment decisions; monitor for treatment-emergent activation.
Stop all medicines without consulting the prescriber.
A past antidepressant trial confirms bipolar disorder.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Bipolar depression needs phase-specific, individualized evidence review. Do not abruptly stop medication or issue a treatment plan from a hypothetical vignette.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person with bipolar disorder taking lithium develops vomiting and diarrhea during a febrile illness and is also taking an NSAID. What is the best educational response?

options.text: No concern; lithium levels never change with illness.
Recognize potential toxicity/interactions and arrange prompt clinical advice/assessment; do not attempt to calculate or change a dose in this self-study course.
Double lithium until symptoms resolve.
Stop every medication permanently.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Intercurrent illness, dehydration and interacting medicines may alter lithium safety. Prompt clinician-directed assessment is appropriate; no dosing instruction is given.
practiceQuestions.domain: NICE CG185; FDA/DailyMed lithium labeling via sources; ABPN pharmacology domain.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person taking valproate is considering pregnancy. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Tell the person to stop valproate immediately.
Use current jurisdiction-specific reproductive-risk guidance and promptly discuss options with the treating specialist; do not abruptly stop without clinical advice.
Assume reproductive risks only apply to females.
Use UK MHRA rules as if they were universal U.S. law.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Valproate has important reproductive risks and changing regulatory measures. Discuss promptly with a qualified clinician and distinguish national policy; abrupt discontinuation may be harmful.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about a positive Mood Disorders Questionnaire is most accurate?

options.text: It confirms bipolar I disorder.
It can be a screening aid, but limited sensitivity/specificity mean a full clinical assessment is needed.
It proves a medication caused mania.
It replaces collateral and longitudinal evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CANMAT/ISBD notes poor sensitivity and specificity; a positive screen can prompt detailed evaluation but is not diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.stem: An older adult develops a new mood/behavior change with cognitive fluctuation and recent medication changes. What is a key next step?

options.text: Assume a first bipolar episode without medical evaluation.
Assess urgent medical/neurologic, medication, substance and cognitive causes along with psychiatric differential in person.
Diagnose cyclothymia from a single visit.
Ignore delirium because the person has a mood history.

practiceQuestions.rationale: New late-life symptoms require consideration of medical, neurologic, medication, substance and cognitive conditions as well as psychiatric illness.
practiceQuestions.domain: NICE CG185; ABPN neurocognitive/neurologic and diagnostic domains.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which intervention is consistent with longitudinal bipolar recovery planning?

options.text: A collaborative plan with patient-valued goals, early warning signs, sleep/rhythm supports, support people as consented, and crisis escalation contacts.
A guarantee that no relapse will occur.
Family contact without consent in all non-emergencies.
Replacing medication and clinician follow-up with a tracking app.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Collaborative, individualized recovery planning and psychoeducation can complement clinical care; no plan guarantees relapse prevention or substitutes for care.

title: Women’s Mental Health and Reproductive Psychiatry Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (institutional post-residency; not ACGME-accredited specialty fellowship as of the cited 2024 field review)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.learnerLevel: Postgraduate physician/psychiatrist or advanced trainee; educational self-study only. Not an entry-to-medicine course.
prerequisites.required: Medical degree and completion of general psychiatry residency-level diagnostic concepts assumed; familiarity with DSM-based assessment, psychopharmacology, suicide-risk assessment and perinatal terminology.
prerequisites.recommended: Prior clinical supervision in psychiatry and reading of ACOG/NICE guideline scope pages. The course does not satisfy clinical hours or supervised training.

objectives: Formulate psychiatric presentations across menstrual, fertility, pregnancy, postpartum, midlife and later reproductive transitions while recognizing heterogeneity and social context.

Recognize suspected postpartum psychosis and medical mimics as urgent; identify need for immediate emergency evaluation.
Differentiate obsessional intrusive thoughts from delusions using insight, meaning and safety assessment without equating thought content with intent.
Apply evidence to PMDD, menopause, trauma, substance-use, eating-disorder and co-occurring presentations.
Communicate inclusive, trauma-informed, culturally responsive plans and interprofessional referral needs.
Critically appraise guidelines and observational studies; identify evidence gaps, limitations and update dates.

assignment.title: Integrated reproductive psychiatry case conference and evidence brief
assignment.instructions: Write a 1,500–2,000 word original formulation for a fictional text-only case spanning one reproductive transition. Include differential, screening-versus-diagnosis distinction, safety, medication/psychotherapy options and uncertainty, patient preferences, inclusive language, equity/access issues, one multidisciplinary referral plan, and a 5-source date-checked evidence table. Do not give a real patient treatment recommendation, reproduce a patient record/image, or assert procedural competency. Add a 10-minute oral teaching outline.

rubric.diagnostic reasoning and differential: 30%; diagnostic uncertainty, context, bipolar/medical mimics where relevant
rubric.safety and escalation: 20%; direct risk assessment, threshold for urgent evaluation, limits
rubric.evidence use: 20%; current primary guidance, date checking, evidence strength and attribution
rubric.shared/inclusive formulation: 15%; values, identity, trauma-informed language, reproductive autonomy
rubric.scholarly clarity: 5%; original writing, citations, no protected patient data

assignment.passingThreshold: Educational benchmark only: 80% rubric points after remediation; not validated for clinical competence.

assessment.format: 12 unit quizzes, original 10-question capstone, case formulation, evidence critique and final self-audit.
assessment.boardAlignment: Question style encourages general psychiatric diagnostic reasoning; no official women’s/reproductive psychiatry board blueprint exists. Not official or recalled ABPN questions.
assessment.rubric: Quizzes assess reasoning, evidence currency, differential, safety and communication. Remediate errors against cited sources; no passing probability or certification inference.

topicGaps: The free public lecture ledger remains far below the 36-hour target; 30.580556 h of suitable recordings with observed runtimes remain to be located. This expansion does not claim course-hour completion.

Fertility, infertility, assisted reproduction and preconception decision-making still lack a verified free lecture with observed runtime; original material is not a substitute for reproductive-endocrinology consultation.

Medication-specific perinatal risk, bipolar illness, lactation pharmacology and current guideline updates need more freely accessible, runtime-verified lectures; the ACOG guideline page flags an Oct 2025 update, while its recommendation content is subscriber-gated.
PMDD prospective diagnosis and PME distinction have source-backed readings and an authored episode, but no newly counted lecture; treatment evidence for PME remains limited.

Trauma, OCD, eating disorders, substance use, later-life menopause, gender-diverse care and reproductive justice remain unevenly represented in verified recorded teaching. A public Michigan substance-use lecture was found but its exact runtime was not observable.

No full public institutional didactic calendar or common national WMH fellowship syllabus is available in the packet; the separate BWH and McLean clinical-fellowship variants and clinical training requirements remain unchanged.
No women’s/reproductive psychiatry certification blueprint or separate ABPN examination is asserted. Mapping remains to the parent Psychiatry competencies and is not a board exam map.
All authored scripts are educational drafts only. No video was rendered or independently clinician-reviewed; human clinical review remains not performed.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.programmeSourceScope: These are two separate official institutional variants listed in the supplied directory packet, with exact packet names retained and official page titles preserved separately. BWH emphasizes integrated women’s/reproductive psychiatry across OB/NICU/C-L/ambulatory care and scholarship; McLean emphasizes levels of care and trauma/eating/substance/personality pathology plus a BWH medical rotation. The training titles are institutional clinical fellowships; they are neither generic directory categories nor research-only/non-physician supplements. The pages require psychiatry residency and clinical licensure, establishing physician clinical intent. A 2024 APA Psychiatric News training review states WMH fellowships were not ACGME accredited at that time; neither official page advertises ACGME accreditation. Institutional pages do not establish a single common national curriculum.

The CPG No. 4 scope on ACOG public page includes mental health screening and diagnosis; full recommendations are inaccessible without subscription.

The two actual institutional page curricula were verified statelessly; proprietary schedules, complete didactics, case volumes, accreditation status beyond available public evidence and outcome data are not claimed.
A 2024 training overview states no ACGME-accredited women’s mental health fellowship programs at publication; this may change and should be rechecked.
Four YouTube videos were counted by unique ID from observed public runtimes. Free viewing is not a rehosting/embed license. A separate video transcript or playlist entry was not counted.
No clinical video from these sources is a validated board review, certification blueprint, or exam predictor.
Human clinical review has not been performed. Independent education conveys no institutional affiliation, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, treatment authority or competency.

topicGaps: The free public lecture ledger remains far below the 36-hour target; 30.580556 h of suitable recordings with observed runtimes remain to be located. This expansion does not claim course-hour completion.

Fertility, infertility, assisted reproduction and preconception decision-making still lack a verified free lecture with observed runtime; original material is not a substitute for reproductive-endocrinology consultation.

Medication-specific perinatal risk, bipolar illness, lactation pharmacology and current guideline updates need more freely accessible, runtime-verified lectures; the ACOG guideline page flags an Oct 2025 update, while its recommendation content is subscriber-gated.

Trauma, OCD, eating disorders, substance use, later-life menopause, gender-diverse care and reproductive justice remain unevenly represented in verified recorded teaching. A public Michigan substance-use lecture was found but its exact runtime was not observable.

No full public institutional didactic calendar or common national WMH fellowship syllabus is available in the packet; the separate BWH and McLean clinical-fellowship variants and clinical training requirements remain unchanged.
No women’s/reproductive psychiatry certification blueprint or separate ABPN examination is asserted. Mapping remains to the parent Psychiatry competencies and is not a board exam map.
All authored scripts are educational drafts only. No video was rendered or independently clinician-reviewed; human clinical review remains not performed.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient at 8 weeks postpartum has a positive depression screen and endorses thoughts of not wanting to live. Which is the best next educational response?

options.text: Treat the screening score as a confirmed diagnosis and defer further interview.
Promptly conduct a direct, clinically appropriate suicide-risk assessment and arrange urgent safety evaluation/referral according to findings; the screen alone is not diagnostic.
Reassure that postpartum mood changes are expected.
Wait until the routine postpartum visit.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening is a gateway to assessment and follow-up; suicidality requires direct risk assessment and action proportionate to risk, not reassurance or score-only diagnosis.
practiceQuestions.domain: Assessment, suicide risk and clinical safety

practiceQuestions.stem: A pregnant patient with prior bipolar I disorder asks about starting an antidepressant for low mood. What principle should guide the assessment?

options.text: Assume unipolar depression because the current complaint is low mood.
Clarify bipolar course, current mixed/manic symptoms, prior response and perinatal risks before choosing a treatment plan with appropriate specialist coordination.
Stop all psychiatric medications immediately because pregnancy is present.
Use a screening instrument alone to decide medication.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Perinatal assessment includes bipolar disorder and individualized treatment; screening does not substitute for diagnostic evaluation. Abrupt medication changes can expose a patient to relapse and require prescriber-led risk-benefit discussion.

practiceQuestions.stem: A new parent develops rapidly fluctuating confusion, fixed beliefs that the infant has been replaced, and very little sleep. What response is most appropriate?

options.text: Schedule routine outpatient follow-up in several weeks.
Treat as possible postpartum psychosis or medical delirium; arrange immediate emergency psychiatric and medical evaluation and protect safety.
Assume intrusive thoughts from OCD because the infant is mentioned.
Diagnose normal postpartum blues.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency. Altered/fluctuating consciousness also requires consideration of delirium and medical mimics. Immediate evaluation is more appropriate than outpatient delay.

practiceQuestions.stem: A postpartum patient reports unwanted, frightening images of accidental infant harm, recognizes the images as inconsistent with her wishes, and repeatedly checks the infant to neutralize distress. Which is the best formulation step?

options.text: Assume delusions and arrange involuntary admission without interview.
Explore obsessions/compulsions, insight, intent, function, psychosis and safety directly; distinguish OCD from psychosis rather than equating thought content with intent.
Avoid asking further questions because this reinforces the thoughts.
Conclude that no risk assessment is needed because insight is present.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts with insight may fit OCD; assessment must still clarify intent, psychosis, impairment and safety. Thought content alone does not establish intent, nor does insight remove the need for assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient stable on an effective medication discovers a pregnancy and asks whether to stop it today. Which counseling framework is most appropriate?

options.text: Recommend automatic abrupt discontinuation to eliminate fetal exposure.
Review prior illness severity and response, risks of treated and untreated illness, medication-specific evidence/uncertainty, patient preferences and monitoring; coordinate a shared plan.
Guarantee that the medication has no fetal or neonatal risk.
Make a decision based only on pregnancy trimester.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Current perinatal guidance frames treatment around illness and medication risks, evidence limits, prior history and shared decision-making. Neither zero-risk claims nor automatic stopping are supported.

practiceQuestions.stem: A breastfeeding patient is prescribed a psychotropic and wants to understand infant exposure. Which resource strategy is best?

options.text: Use an up-to-date drug-specific lactation source such as LactMed alongside clinical context, infant factors, maternal benefit and current guideline advice.
Assume every medication is contraindicated during breastfeeding.
Use a single old general statement for all drugs and infants.
Advise dose changes without consulting the prescriber.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Lactation evidence is drug-specific and must be interpreted in context; clinical sources need updating and individualized clinician discussion. The NCBI page could not be read in this research session, so learners should access its current monograph directly.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient describes mood symptoms that reliably emerge before menstruation and remit shortly after menses, but no daily ratings have yet been recorded. What is a sound next diagnostic step?

options.text: Confirm PMDD from retrospective recall alone.
Collect prospective daily symptom ratings across cycles and assess impairment and alternative explanations before finalizing a diagnosis.
Assume symptoms are caused by hormone levels and order hormone tests as the only assessment.
Diagnose bipolar disorder from cyclicity alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Prospective symptom tracking helps verify a cycle-linked pattern and distinguish PMDD from premenstrual exacerbation or other conditions; diagnosis is not established by retrospective pattern alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 52-year-old reports new low mood, insomnia, hot flashes and concentration difficulty during irregular cycles. Which formulation best avoids diagnostic error?

options.text: Attribute all symptoms to menopause without psychiatric assessment.
Assess mood/anxiety, sleep, function, medical/reproductive context and patient goals; use current menopause guidance and coordinate individualized options.
Assume hormone therapy is always the treatment for depression.
Dismiss cognitive symptoms as inevitable aging.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The menopause transition can involve multiple symptoms, but symptoms warrant individualized assessment. Current NICE menopause guidance was updated in April 2026 and supports care decisions based on the patient’s needs and context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient’s mental health screen is negative at one visit but a relative reports marked functional deterioration. What is the best general principle?

options.text: Use the screening result to rule out illness.
Integrate history, function, collateral when appropriate and consented, clinical interview and follow-up; screens do not replace assessment.
Wait for another positive questionnaire before offering assessment.
Assume the relative’s report establishes a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening is not a diagnostic substitute; assessment incorporates symptoms, functioning, context and appropriate follow-up while respecting consent/confidentiality.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee is asked whether a one-year Women’s Mental Health fellowship confers a separate ABPN certificate. What is the best answer based on current sources?

options.text: Yes, completion automatically grants ABPN reproductive psychiatry certification.
No separate ABPN women’s/reproductive psychiatry subspecialty exam is listed; fellowship training is distinct from board certification and eligibility.
The fellowship guarantees eligibility for every ABPN subspecialty exam.
All hospital fellowship titles are automatically ACGME-accredited.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPN’s current roster lists defined psychiatry subspecialty examinations, not women’s/reproductive psychiatry; a 2024 training-pathways article reported no ACGME-accredited WMH programmes at that time. Confirm directly with ABPN/ACGME for any later change.

title: Structural Heart Disease Fellowship
level: Institution-specific advanced clinical physician fellowship (MGB-listed; separate accreditation status not established by the public page)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Intended level: cardiologists/interventional cardiologists and advanced physician learners who already have graduate clinical training; not entry-level medical students or independent procedure training.

MGB’s published prerequisite for its fellowship is completion of three years of ACGME-accredited Cardiovascular Disease fellowship plus a one-year ACGME-accredited Interventional Cardiology fellowship. This course does not verify credentials or confer entry eligibility.
Baseline knowledge: valve physiology/severity, echocardiography and cardiac CT/CMR concepts, hemodynamics, coronary/interventional safety, trial literacy and shared decision-making.
objectives: Apply a structured, uncertainty-aware approach to structural-heart referral, diagnostic confirmation and Heart Team case selection.
Compare aortic, mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary and septal structural therapies while separating guideline-level indications, device-label constraints and local expert judgment.
Interpret the role and limits of multimodality imaging and invasive hemodynamics in a treatment question.
Recognize complications, postprocedure surveillance needs, prosthetic dysfunction differentials, quality-improvement opportunities and evidence limitations.
Map knowledge and cognitive skills to current published ABIM interventional cardiology and cardiovascular disease blueprints without implying board readiness.

topicGaps: Verified coverage: 13 unique public specialty recordings with directly observed player runtimes total 10h43m12s (10.72 h); the 36-hour video floor remains short by exactly 25h16m48s (25.28 h). A 57:30 ACC TAVI-complication lecture formerly of unknown duration is now verified from its public player plus ACC event page. Nine new recordings were added. Neither scripted teaching nor planned minutes count.

Seven legacy specialty recordings still have unknown public runtime/access and remain uncounted: yt--EsAKaYzewU, yt-H7HQv5OUj-w, yt-CAOlCyHn9dA, yt-Ih-PCZbr870, yt-sVRVbo0DLXM, yt-TI0N82EECRs, and yt-vw6i_OxsBMg. The patient-oriented TAVR overview remains labeled supplementary and is separately excluded from specialty hours; other legacy candidates are retained in their original categories with caveats. No runtime is inferred from search listings.

Even with the new mitral, tricuspid, PFO, LAAO imaging, prosthetic-valve, CT, and TAVI-complication recordings, substantial board-level coverage lacks verified long-form video: pulmonary valve/congenital intervention, ASD/PDA, LAAO indication/antithrombotic follow-up, PVL, HCM septal reduction, postprocedure endocarditis/thrombosis and surveillance, radiation/contrast, comprehensive complication simulation and QI. Seek complete academic/society sources. Existing written unit content/questions remain; this list is source-coverage, not a deletion of curriculum.

The CT lecture and mitral/tricuspid joint talk date from 2017 and 2020; the PFO webinar is from 2019; UW TR grand rounds and ACC TAVI webinar are from 2021. They are useful conceptual recordings only and do not substitute for current 2025 guidance, primary trial publications, current U.S./local guidance, or device instructions for use. The 2024 TR lecture page shows technical set-up and introductions in its displayed runtime; the 2020 mitral/tricuspid video begins after missing opening minutes. Full displayed recording runtimes, not reconstructed lecture-only durations, were counted and those qualifications are recorded.

officialProgrammes.name: Structural Heart Disease Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official MGB page describes a physician fellowship at Massachusetts General Hospital, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and the W. Roxbury VA; entry prerequisite: three years of ACGME-accredited Cardiovascular Disease fellowship plus one year of ACGME-accredited Interventional Cardiology fellowship. Publicly stated experience includes aortic, mitral and tricuspid interventions; PFO/ASD/PDA closure; LAA occlusion; PVL closure; congenital interventions; QI and journal club. medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet and current official MGB page support one exact institutional variant: Mass General Brigham, Structural Heart Disease Fellowship, across MGH/BWH/W. Roxbury VA sites. No separate Harvard Medical School or Johns Hopkins structural-heart program variant was independently verified for this item. This is a clinical physician fellowship, not a generic directory category or research/non-physician supplement. The public page is an institutional offering, not an ABIM board or, by itself, evidence of separate ACGME accreditation.
sourceCaveats: Official institutional page is dynamic and should be rechecked for programme details and current AY recruitment. It states stated procedure counts for participating institutions, not individual fellow case logs.

ABIM policy and exam blueprints change; this course maps to versions retrieved 2026-10-07 and must be reviewed against the current board source. No separate SHD board exam was identified, not a guarantee none will ever exist.

2025 ESC/EACTS guideline is international; users in the United States must also consult current U.S. guidelines, FDA device labeling and local Heart Team policy. The ACC/AHA valve guideline item included here is 2020, and should not be portrayed as newer than the 2025 ESC update.
