topicGaps: Verified coverage: 13 unique public specialty recordings with directly observed player runtimes total 10h43m12s (10.72 h); the 36-hour video floor remains short by exactly 25h16m48s (25.28 h). A 57:30 ACC TAVI-complication lecture formerly of unknown duration is now verified from its public player plus ACC event page. Nine new recordings were added. Neither scripted teaching nor planned minutes count.

Seven legacy specialty recordings still have unknown public runtime/access and remain uncounted: yt--EsAKaYzewU, yt-H7HQv5OUj-w, yt-CAOlCyHn9dA, yt-Ih-PCZbr870, yt-sVRVbo0DLXM, yt-TI0N82EECRs, and yt-vw6i_OxsBMg. The patient-oriented TAVR overview remains labeled supplementary and is separately excluded from specialty hours; other legacy candidates are retained in their original categories with caveats. No runtime is inferred from search listings.

Even with the new mitral, tricuspid, PFO, LAAO imaging, prosthetic-valve, CT, and TAVI-complication recordings, substantial board-level coverage lacks verified long-form video: pulmonary valve/congenital intervention, ASD/PDA, LAAO indication/antithrombotic follow-up, PVL, HCM septal reduction, postprocedure endocarditis/thrombosis and surveillance, radiation/contrast, comprehensive complication simulation and QI. Seek complete academic/society sources. Existing written unit content/questions remain; this list is source-coverage, not a deletion of curriculum.

The CT lecture and mitral/tricuspid joint talk date from 2017 and 2020; the PFO webinar is from 2019; UW TR grand rounds and ACC TAVI webinar are from 2021. They are useful conceptual recordings only and do not substitute for current 2025 guidance, primary trial publications, current U.S./local guidance, or device instructions for use. The 2024 TR lecture page shows technical set-up and introductions in its displayed runtime; the 2020 mitral/tricuspid video begins after missing opening minutes. Full displayed recording runtimes, not reconstructed lecture-only durations, were counted and those qualifications are recorded.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A referral arrives for a patient with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis. The echo measurements are internally discordant, stroke volume is low, and the patient has several competing illnesses. What is the best educational next step before recommending a transcatheter procedure?

options.text: Choose a valve platform from the single peak velocity value.
Reconcile disease severity and flow state, obtain appropriate confirmatory assessment, and review goals/risks with the multidisciplinary Heart Team.
Assume low flow proves that intervention cannot help.
Use an age cutoff alone to choose TAVR over surgery.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Discordant low-flow/low-gradient findings require integrated assessment rather than a single-value or age-only rule. Guidelines and advanced-training statements emphasize multimodality assessment, alternatives, patient goals, and Heart Team judgment.
practiceQuestions.domain: IC structural case selection / CVD valvular disease

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner compares the MGB structural-heart fellowship with ACGME training. Which statement is supported by the official MGB page?

options.text: The structural-heart year replaces the three-year cardiovascular disease and one-year interventional cardiology prerequisites.
The page requires three years of ACGME-accredited cardiovascular disease training and one year of ACGME-accredited interventional cardiology training before entry.
Completion automatically confers ABIM structural-heart certification.
The page confirms that the structural-heart fellowship itself has a separate ABMS board exam.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The institutional page explicitly names those prior fellowships as requirements. It does not establish a structural-specific ABMS certification or board examination.

practiceQuestions.stem: TTE suggests a new high gradient across a transcatheter prosthetic valve. The patient is stable, and prior baseline images are available. Which first approach best reflects the prosthetic-valve imaging guidance?

options.text: Compare a comprehensive current TTE with baseline and then select TEE, CT, or CMR if morphology/function remains uncertain.
Proceed directly to reintervention based on the number alone.
Use CMR as the required first-line test in every case.
Exclude thrombosis if Doppler flow is detectable.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASE identifies echocardiography, especially TTE, as first-line, with TEE/CT/CMR as complementary tests for selected questions. A new gradient is a finding requiring contextual evaluation, not an intervention indication by itself.

practiceQuestions.stem: A published case describes sudden hemodynamic collapse with incomplete expansion of a self-expanding TAVR device. What is the appropriate learner use of this case?

options.text: Treat it as proof that all self-expanding valves should be avoided.
Identify the reported event, discuss the safety/diagnostic questions with the team, and avoid generalizing one case into an efficacy rule.
Copy the case imaging into a new course deck because it is public.
Use the narrative as a credential for independent valve implantation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Published case reports support learning from events but do not independently establish comparative effectiveness or competence. SCAI content remains copyrighted; linking is appropriate, not rehosting.

practiceQuestions.stem: When preparing to review CT for possible transfemoral TAVR, which group of questions most appropriately structures the discussion?

options.text: Annular/root dimensions, coronary and aortic-root relationships, and iliofemoral access feasibility/risks.
Only ejection fraction and calcium score.
Only aortic valve area; CT cannot inform access.
Only device company preference.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CT planning addresses annular/root geometry, coronary-obstruction risk, vascular access and other anatomy relevant to procedural planning. Specific measurement and device decisions require current protocols, labeled devices, and expert review.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has PFO on TTE and unexplained hypoxemia after surgery. What is the most defensible initial reasoning step before recommending closure?

options.text: Assume every PFO is causal and schedule closure.
Evaluate the clinical syndrome and alternative shunt/pulmonary causes, then characterize shunt physiology and anatomy with appropriate testing.
Use PFO prevalence to prove the PFO caused hypoxemia.
Ignore imaging because shunt symptoms are diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Anatomic PFO is common and does not itself establish causality. Published cases emphasize shunt evaluation and alternative explanations before closure decisions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees a webinar listed on an industry webpage that requires sign-up and functional cookies. How should it be treated in an independent free-view video-hour ledger if runtime has not been observed?

options.text: Count one hour because most webinars are about an hour.
Count it if the topic matches, even if access requires enrollment.
Record it as access-restricted/unknown duration and exclude it from verified free hours.
Estimate the runtime from the page title.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Contract rules require free-access confirmation and observed runtime; estimates and login-gated content are excluded. The Abbott page asks visitors to subscribe and accept functional cookies to watch.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with severe MR has substantial comorbidity and symptoms despite therapy. Which recommendation framework is most appropriate for an educational discussion?

options.text: Select TEER based solely on MR grade.
Integrate MR mechanism/severity, LV status, symptoms, anatomy, expected benefit, surgical/transcatheter/medical options, and patient goals in a Heart Team review.
Use one 3D TEE view as a complete selection rule.
Assume secondary MR and primary MR have identical criteria.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Intervention selection requires mechanism, clinical status, anatomy and alternatives; current guidelines emphasize Heart Team and patient-centred decisions, and imaging modalities are complementary.
practiceQuestions.domain: IC noncoronary disease case selection / CVD valvular disease

practiceQuestions.stem: After a large-bore structural intervention, a patient develops hypotension and a falling hemoglobin. Which course objective is most relevant?

options.text: Escalate concern for bleeding/access injury and hemodynamic compromise using local emergency protocols and multidisciplinary help.
Assume the change is expected and wait until routine follow-up.
Treat hypotension as evidence of valve thrombosis only.
Use this course to authorize independent emergency procedural management.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Large-bore access injury and bleeding are important structural-heart hazards; early recognition and supervised institutional response are core safety themes. This self-study material cannot authorize clinical action.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes board preparation for the Structural Heart Disease Fellowship curriculum?

options.text: ABIM offers a separate structural-heart certification examination.
ABIM has an Interventional Cardiology certification examination with structural/valvular case-selection content; this is not a separate structural-heart board.
The MGB fellowship guarantees eligibility for all boards.
An online self-study course can satisfy ACGME procedure requirements.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM lists Interventional Cardiology certification and blueprint domains including structural/valvular case selection. No separate structural-heart exam is identified in ABIM certification lists. Exam access/eligibility is controlled by board rules, not by this course.

title: Thoracic Anesthesiology Fellowship
level: Non-ACGME clinical physician fellowship-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Graduated physician with anesthesiology residency-level knowledge; intended primarily for anesthesiologists, not a substitute for their prerequisites.
Working knowledge of airway anatomy, cardiopulmonary physiology, mechanical ventilation, pharmacology, monitoring and perioperative medicine.
Ability to appraise guidelines and understand that passive learning cannot confer technical competence or clinical privileges.
objectives: Analyze common thoracic operations and construct a conceptual perioperative plan with contingencies.
Explain lung isolation, bronchoscopic confirmation principles and causes of failure.
Reason through OLV physiology and individualized protective ventilation tradeoffs.
Structure an evidence-grounded differential and team response to thoracic intraoperative hypoxemia.
Integrate pulmonary reserve, hemodynamics, regional analgesia, enhanced recovery and postoperative disposition.
Summarize lung-transplant phases, ECLS considerations and reperfusion risk from consensus sources.
Critically assess evidence, board/accreditation status and rights for clinical learning materials.

units.title: Thoracic surgery, anesthetic plan, and safe systems
objectives: Describe core thoracic operations and map operation/site to airway, ventilation, position, access and postoperative disposition implications.
Create a multidisciplinary preinduction plan with explicit decision points, equipment, escalation and handoff.
Distinguish educational knowledge from credentialed performance of procedures.
topics: VATS/robotic/open resection, esophagectomy, airway resection, mediastinal procedures and transplant; positioning; equipment; consent and communication.
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED/APPLIED general anesthesiology domains (exam-level conceptual alignment only); MGB stated clinical focus, not a published board blueprint.
casePractice: Use MGB page’s procedure list as a checklist, not as evidence of case numbers or competency.
assessment: Submit a one-page case-conference plan with patient risks, proposed conduct, contingency branches, stop rules and team roles. Rubric: risk identification 30%, coherent branching 30%, evidence/uncertainty 20%, communication/safety 20%.

units.title: Preoperative pulmonary reserve and risk communication
objectives: Interpret FEV1, DLCO, predicted postoperative function, exercise capacity and gas exchange as complementary rather than interchangeable measures.
Identify questions for thoracic surgery/pulmonology when functional reserve is limited.
Communicate uncertainty without converting a screening threshold into an automatic eligibility decision.
topics: COPD, ILD, oxygenation, exercise tolerance, CPET, ppoFEV1/ppoDLCO, frailty/nutrition, smoking cessation, risk-benefit and shared decision-making.
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED: respiratory physiology and perioperative risk; no specialty exam blueprint for thoracic anesthesia.
casePractice: Calculate a provided ppo measure only when supplied data permit; compare to relevant contemporary local guidance; state why the 2014 review’s threshold algorithm must be checked against updated guidance.
assessment: Interpret a fictional preoperative panel and write a 250-word consultation note. Rubric: correct interpretation 35%, missing-data queries 25%, calibrated risk statement 25%, citations 15%.

units.title: Thoracic airway evaluation and difficult airway planning
objectives: Compare double-lumen tube (DLT) and bronchial blocker tradeoffs and choose an initial plan for a described airway/surgical context.
Use a structured difficult-airway strategy, including awake approach consideration and rescue options.
Anticipate airway loss, obstruction, bleeding, airway injury and fire-related risks during airway procedures.
topics: Airway anatomy, DLT size/side, bronchial blockers, flexible bronchoscopy, exchange catheters, mediastinal mass physiology, tracheal stenosis, rigid bronchoscopy coordination.
boardDomains: ABA BASIC/ADVANCED/APPLIED airway and equipment; MGB’s posted technical skills (not proof of course competency).
casePractice: Review the openly linked mediastinal-mass case as a decision-analysis exercise; do not copy the patient image or treat a case report as universal guidance.
assessment: Record a structured verbal airway plan from a fictional vignette, including triggers to pause/abort. Rubric: primary plan 25%, backup/rescue 30%, pathophysiology 20%, communication 15%, limits 10%.

units.title: Lung isolation devices, placement confirmation and troubleshooting
objectives: Explain DLT and blocker mechanics and their failure modes.
Outline a safe confirmation checklist using flexible bronchoscopy and reassessment after repositioning or surgical manipulation.
Differentiate malposition, obstruction, leak and inadequate collapse from other causes of high airway pressure.
topics: Left/right DLT; bronchial blockers; bronchoscopic landmarks; lateral positioning; tube fixation, cuff pressures, suction and device exchange.
boardDomains: ABA BASIC airway anatomy/equipment; advanced thoracic airway learning aligned to MGB rotation description.
casePractice: Use schematic-only airway diagrams or linked authentic material under its displayed license. No procedural competence is inferred from online viewing.
assessment: Submit an annotated written bronchoscopy-view interpretation using a licensed public teaching image if available; otherwise a labeled schematic. Rubric: landmarks 30%, device position reasoning 30%, failure recognition 25%, rights/citation 15%.

units.title: One-lung ventilation physiology and lung-protective strategy
objectives: Relate shunt, V/Q mismatch and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) to expected OLV gas exchange.
Compare tidal volume, PEEP, recruitment, FiO2 and hemodynamic tradeoffs using source-specific qualifiers.
Recognize that settings should be individualized to patient, surgery and current institutional guidance.
topics: HPV, lateral position/perfusion, shunt, ventilator modes, ideal body weight, PEEP/recruitment, hyperoxia, surgical exposure and dependent-lung injury.
boardDomains: ABA BASIC respiratory physiology/ventilation; content aligned to adult thoracic anesthesia, not a separate exam.
casePractice: Compare 2019 ERAS guidance and 2023 review; note variation across sources rather than teaching one universal ventilator recipe.
assessment: Write a 5-minute chalk-talk explaining physiology and choose a defensible starting approach for a fictional case. Rubric: mechanism 30%, individualized strategy 30%, hemodynamic tradeoffs 20%, evidence reconciliation 20%.

units.title: Intraoperative hypoxemia and crisis management
objectives: Use a structured approach to abrupt versus gradual hypoxemia during OLV.
Prioritize communication, immediate oxygenation/ventilation restoration when indicated, confirmation of isolation-device position and cause-directed response.
Identify important differentials including hemorrhage, device malposition, pneumothorax, gas embolism, bronchospasm, RV failure/PE and shunt.
topics: Alarm validation, two-lung ventilation, bronchoscopy, recruitment/PEEP, surgical field, hemodynamics, CPAP/operative-lung oxygen strategies, ECMO planning limits.
boardDomains: ABA APPLIED oral/OSCE reasoning; crisis management conceptual alignment; not certification content.
casePractice: Analyze published case reports to compare decisions; do not endorse isolated rescue interventions as universal protocols.
assessment: Complete an event timeline and root-cause differential for a fictional OLV desaturation. Rubric: immediate stabilization 30%, diagnostic sequence 25%, team communication 20%, cause-specific branches 15%, evidence 10%.

units.title: Hemodynamic monitoring, right-heart physiology, and TEE concepts
objectives: Explain interactions among intrathoracic pressure, venous return, PVR, RV function, and pulmonary artery clamping.
Identify perioperative clues warranting consideration of RV failure or pulmonary embolism and escalation to expert echocardiography.
Interpret basic hemodynamic trends without overclaiming from any single measurement.
topics: RV afterload, hypoxia/hypercarbia/acidosis, pulmonary hypertension, arterial/central access indications, TEE role, lung isolation and surgical events.
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED cardiovascular/respiratory reasoning; TEE concepts are didactic and not credentialing.
casePractice: For transplant, link consensus and openly accessible review; do not use illustrative figures without license review.
assessment: Explain a fictional hemodynamic trend to a multidisciplinary team; state what additional data would change the differential. Rubric: physiology 35%, differential 25%, data limitations 20%, communication 20%.

units.title: Regional analgesia and enhanced recovery after thoracic surgery
objectives: Compare thoracic epidural, paravertebral, erector spinae and serratus plane options in context of operation, contraindications and local expertise.
Summarize procedure-specific VATS recommendations and distinguish them from open-thoracotomy evidence.
Connect analgesia with coughing, mobilization, respiratory function, opioid minimization and multimodal adverse-effect assessment.
topics: Acute pain, blocks, anticoagulation/contraindications, PONV, multimodal analgesia, ERAS, fluid therapy, normothermia and early mobilization.
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED/APPLIED perioperative analgesia and acute care reasoning.
casePractice: PROSPECT VATS evidence supports basic analgesia and recommends paravertebral or erector spinae as first-choice options; individualize and check current update/local protocol.
assessment: Create a one-page comparison matrix for VATS versus thoracotomy with evidence and caveats. Rubric: procedure distinction 25%, evidence fidelity 30%, safety/contraindications 25%, multimodal recovery linkage 20%.

units.title: Robotic, airway, esophageal and complex thoracic procedures
objectives: Anticipate anesthetic constraints for robotic positioning, restricted access, CO2 insufflation and emergency undocking.
Describe coordination issues during rigid bronchoscopy, airway resection and jet/cross-field ventilation in conceptual terms.
Relate esophagectomy and mediastinal operations to aspiration, ventilation, analgesia and postoperative respiratory risk.
topics: Robotic docking/undocking plans; airway laser/fire risks; rigid bronchoscopy; surgical ventilation; esophagectomy; one-lung ventilation; emergency conversion.
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED/APPLIED equipment, airway and perioperative planning domains.
casePractice: Use MGB posted procedure list to scope learning; institution-specific room workflows are not publicly available and no local steps should be inferred.
assessment: Submit a multidisciplinary briefing with emergency access/undocking pathway for a fictional robotic case. Rubric: access contingencies 30%, physiologic tradeoffs 25%, team roles 25%, explicit limits 20%.

units.title: Lung transplantation, extracorporeal support, and reperfusion
objectives: Outline major anesthetic phases in lung transplantation and relate changing physiology to surgical milestones.
Explain why extracorporeal support may be planned for selected high-risk situations and distinguish it from a generic rescue response.
Describe primary graft dysfunction surveillance concepts and protective post-reperfusion management using current consensus sources.
topics: Recipient end-stage lung disease, donor-recipient matching concepts, induction, one-lung ventilation, PA clamping, ECMO/CPB distinction, reperfusion injury, PGD, airway exchange.
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED cardiovascular/respiratory; no dedicated thoracic-anesthesia board.
casePractice: MGB page says shared transplant call; this does not establish transplant eligibility, independent competence or local volume.
assessment: Create a phase-based transplant map and identify when the source supports uncertainty rather than fixed settings. Rubric: phases 25%, physiology 25%, ECLS distinction 20%, source calibration 20%, handoff 10%.

units.title: Postoperative disposition, complications and quality improvement
objectives: Identify common immediate postoperative threats after pulmonary resection and link them to surveillance/disposition planning.
Apply ERAS principles to mobilization, pulmonary hygiene, fluid balance, PONV, chest-drain context and escalation.
Use a structured debrief/quality framework without assigning causation unsupported by evidence.
topics: Respiratory failure, atelectasis, bleeding, air leak, arrhythmia, aspiration, pain, delirium, VTE prevention, handoff, human factors and QI.
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED/APPLIED postoperative care and crisis management.
casePractice: Program-specific ICU rotations and optional experiences described by MGB are institutional training experiences; independent learners cannot perform or receive supervised clinical exposure.
assessment: Review a fictional postoperative event and submit an SBAR handoff plus two measurable QI ideas. Rubric: threats/escalation 30%, handoff 25%, feasible measures 25%, source/uncertainty 20%.

units.title: Evidence appraisal, ethics, communication and board-style synthesis
objectives: Appraise recommendation strength, population and limitations across guideline, review and case report evidence.
Separate board certification, ACGME accreditation, programme-level claims and individual competency.
Solve integrated vignettes with prioritized differential, management rationale and a clear stop/escalation boundary.
topics: Evidence hierarchy, consent, human factors, patient-centered communication, licensure, professionalism, test construction, reflective learning and limitations.
boardDomains: ABA BASIC/ADVANCED/APPLIED format domains in general; no separate thoracic examination or published thoracic blueprint found.
casePractice: Independent self-tests are educational only; no official exam items are reproduced or claimed.
assessment: Take a 10-question original assessment and write error analysis with 3 knowledge/decision gaps. Rubric: accuracy 40%, reasoning 30%, evidence use 20%, calibration 10%.

assignment.capstone: Create an evidence-cited multidisciplinary conference packet for a fictional adult elective lung-resection case. Include preoperative data questions, airway/lung-isolation options, OLV considerations, analgesia, hypoxemia decision tree, postoperative handoff, uncertainty register and source/rights audit. Do not include real patient data, individualized treatment advice, drug/dose prescriptions, or instructions to perform procedures.

assessment.formative: 12 unit assignments and retrieval practice; faculty/qualified clinician review is recommended before any educational use beyond personal study.
assessment.summative: 10 original practice questions plus capstone; completion is not a validated predictor of board performance. No minimum score implies competence, passing, board eligibility or patient-care readiness.
assessment.rubric: Question rationales assessed for evidence fidelity, prioritization and explicit uncertainty. Human clinical review not performed.

studyHours.planDescription: Proposed independent-study workload only (not clinical training): 12 units × 12 learner hours each, including approximately 3 h reading, 3 h planned-recording time only after future production, 3 h case/assignment work, 2 h recall/questions, 1 h synthesis per unit. As recordings do not currently exist/count, the 36 planned viewing hours are not presently available; learners should use reading/case study tasks instead and total realized hours will differ. No rotation, procedure, supervised case or patient encounter hours are included.

mapping.institution: Mass General Brigham (MGB; clinical sites named: Massachusetts General Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital)
mapping.name: Thoracic Anesthesia Fellowship Program
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official programme page calls it non-ACGME-accredited, intended for anesthesiologists, and describes a 12-month individualized fellowship with dual-site MGH/BWH rotations, thoracic ORs 6–8 months, optional thoracic ICU/TEE/elective, weekly teaching, academic day, lung isolation/airway/regional techniques and transplant call. These are institutional training elements, not self-study equivalents or verified competency/case-volume claims.

topicGaps: At review, 12 distinct public recording IDs have observed durations and public source pages; the deduplicated ledger totals 45369 seconds (12.6025 hours: 12h 36m 09s), including 1.3964 foundation hours and 11.2061 specialty hours.
The 36-hour target remains unmet: 23.3975 hours (23h 23m 51s) of video time are still unverified. Original scripts and the production-plan target minutes are not recordings and count as zero hours.

Public recordings do not cover every fellowship topic with equal depth. Direct evidence is especially limited for institution-specific workflows, robotic emergency access, detailed thoracic regional techniques, TEE competence, transplant-center ECLS decisions, and supervised procedural practice; original planned modules cannot replace clinical rotations or local protocols.

Several recordings are historical or broad educational resources. The University of Kentucky five-part review is a 2019 keyword review, the ERAS/ESTS guideline is from 2019, and video recommendations must be checked against current sources; none establishes current board blueprint coverage.

A candidate OLV video appeared in search metadata as 22:55 but its fetched watch page returned ‘Video unavailable’; it is excluded. Existing five unknown-duration candidate items remain uncounted. Public video availability and playback can change, and not every player could be interactively tested without stateful access.
No recording, script, or independent course can establish clinical skill, case volume, certification, eligibility, privilege, or patient-care readiness. Human clinician review has not been performed.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass General Brigham (MGB; clinical sites named: Massachusetts General Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital)
officialProgrammes.name: Thoracic Anesthesia Fellowship Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official programme page calls it non-ACGME-accredited, intended for anesthesiologists, and describes a 12-month individualized fellowship with dual-site MGH/BWH rotations, thoracic ORs 6–8 months, optional thoracic ICU/TEE/elective, weekly teaching, academic day, lung isolation/airway/regional techniques and transplant call. These are institutional training elements, not self-study equivalents or verified competency/case-volume claims.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet corresponds to a specific official MGB physician clinical fellowship page, not a generic directory category, research-only job, or nonphysician supplement. It is not combined with MGH or BWH Adult Cardiothoracic Anesthesiology fellowships, which are separate ACGME-accredited programme variants. The MGB page explicitly says non-ACGME and thoracic focus; physician credential details/selection criteria beyond its public page should be confirmed directly with programme. The page says experience-dependent 12 months and prior experience contingent; do not infer general eligibility.
sourceCaveats: The programme page’s stated clinical experience and annual surgical case volume are institutional claims and do not prove fellow case counts, specific board eligibility, or learner competency. This curriculum does not repeat the page’s case-volume statement as a learner benchmark.

The MGB non-ACGME Thoracic Anesthesia Fellowship differs from separately listed ACGME Adult Cardiothoracic Anesthesiology programs at MGH/BWH. Do not infer equivalence, combined enrollment or board outcomes.
The ABA current exam directory checked has an Adult Cardiac Anesthesiology exam but no distinct Thoracic Anesthesiology exam. No independent thoracic board is named.

Stateless public metadata could not provide reliable YouTube player durations/free-playback status for five candidate videos; some metadata endpoints returned extraction errors or bot/login challenge. No login, browser, bypass, or estimate used. No video counted.
2026-10-07 is the review date; clinical practice and programme/board requirements can change. Recheck primary sources before use.
Clinical human review is not performed; no accreditation, affiliation, supervised training, licensure, procedure competency, certification, or passing guarantee is provided.

The case reports are authentic published clinical reports, but article-specific consent/de-identification disclosures were not independently reviewed. Only links are supplied; no patient records or images are copied. Learners should follow source terms and institutional privacy rules.

The 36-hour target remains unmet: 23.3975 hours (23h 23m 51s) of video time are still unverified. Original scripts and the production-plan target minutes are not recordings and count as zero hours.

Public recordings do not cover every fellowship topic with equal depth. Direct evidence is especially limited for institution-specific workflows, robotic emergency access, detailed thoracic regional techniques, TEE competence, transplant-center ECLS decisions, and supervised procedural practice; original planned modules cannot replace clinical rotations or local protocols.

Several recordings are historical or broad educational resources. The University of Kentucky five-part review is a 2019 keyword review, the ERAS/ESTS guideline is from 2019, and video recommendations must be checked against current sources; none establishes current board blueprint coverage.

A candidate OLV video appeared in search metadata as 22:55 but its fetched watch page returned ‘Video unavailable’; it is excluded. Existing five unknown-duration candidate items remain uncounted. Public video availability and playback can change, and not every player could be interactively tested without stateful access.
No recording, script, or independent course can establish clinical skill, case volume, certification, eligibility, privilege, or patient-care readiness. Human clinician review has not been performed.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: During OLV, SpO2 falls abruptly with rising peak pressure and an abnormal capnogram after lateral positioning. What is the most appropriate immediate sequence?

options.text: Continue OLV and increase tidal volume
Notify team/surgeon, restore two-lung ventilation with high FiO2 while evaluating, and urgently confirm isolation-device position with bronchoscopy
Administer a pulmonary vasodilator before checking airway position
Remove the DLT without a backup airway plan

practiceQuestions.rationale: Abrupt, severe desaturation requires immediate team notification and restoration of oxygenation/ventilation while the cause is sought; device malposition is a key reversible cause and bronchoscopic confirmation is recommended. A specific rescue drug should not precede stabilization and diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner presents a 2019 ERAS source recommending a protective OLV approach. Which statement best reflects evidence use?

options.text: A single ventilator setting is mandatory for every OLV case
Protective strategies are supported, but settings such as tidal volume/PEEP should be individualized and source recommendations reconciled with current local guidance
High tidal volumes are always safer because oxygenation improves
PEEP should never be used during OLV

practiceQuestions.rationale: ERAS recommends lung-protective strategies; the review literature notes individual physiology and competing oxygenation/hemodynamic effects. Avoid turning ranges into an inflexible universal prescription.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with a difficult airway needs lung isolation for thoracic surgery. What is a sound planning principle?

options.text: Choose a DLT in every patient because blockers are contraindicated
Consider relative advantages of a bronchial blocker with a single-lumen tube, planned awake airway strategy when indicated, backup oxygenation and experienced team; confirm position bronchoscopically
Proceed with standard induction and defer airway planning until after positioning
Use a blocker without confirming placement

practiceQuestions.rationale: A blocker can be useful when DLT placement is difficult; the airway approach must be individualized with a difficult-airway strategy and flexible bronchoscopic confirmation. This is conceptual education, not a procedural instruction.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which interpretation of the ABA website is correct for thoracic anesthesiology?

options.text: A separate ABA Thoracic Anesthesiology certification exam is listed
Thoracic anesthesia is the same as ABA Adult Cardiac Anesthesiology certification
ABA lists Adult Cardiac Anesthesiology among subspecialty exams, but not a separate Thoracic Anesthesiology exam
The MGB non-ACGME fellowship automatically confers ABA subspecialty certification

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABA’s current list includes Adult Cardiac Anesthesiology, among other listed subspecialty exams, but does not list a thoracic anesthesia examination. Completing a non-ACGME programme does not confer board certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: In evaluating a lung-resection candidate, why are FEV1 and DLCO both relevant?

options.text: They measure identical function, so only one should be used
They provide complementary information on airflow and gas-transfer reserve; risk interpretation may need predicted postoperative estimates and exercise assessment
A normal FEV1 excludes increased perioperative risk
A threshold in an older review alone determines surgical candidacy

practiceQuestions.rationale: The open review discusses spirometry and DLCO as initial complementary tests, with additional exercise assessment when reduced. Its thresholds are historical guidance and must not replace current multidisciplinary/local evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient undergoing VATS asks for a pain plan. Which answer is best supported by the 2022 PROSPECT review?

options.text: Routine thoracic epidural is first-line for all VATS

Basic paracetamol/NSAID or COX-2 therapy and a paravertebral or erector spinae plane block as a first-choice regional option, with opioids generally as rescue, subject to contraindications and local practice
Opioids should be scheduled as the only modality
No regional technique is recommended

practiceQuestions.rationale: The VATS-specific systematic review recommends basic analgesia and identifies paravertebral or erector spinae plane block as first-choice options; opioids are reserved for rescue. Patient-specific contraindications and current institutional policy still apply.

practiceQuestions.stem: During OLV a patient with pulmonary hypertension develops rising CVP, hypotension, hypercarbia and acidosis. Which interpretation should be prioritized?

options.text: Acute RV failure is plausible and merits urgent assessment of RV function and reversible triggers
This is always DLT malposition
A rising CVP excludes right-heart dysfunction
Acidosis has no relevance to RV afterload

practiceQuestions.rationale: The OLV review identifies acute RV failure as a cause of hypoxemia/instability, particularly with pulmonary hypertension; hypercarbia and acidosis can worsen pulmonary vascular load. Expert escalation and cause evaluation are required.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about lung transplantation anesthesia is accurate?

options.text: Routine ECMO is required for every transplant
Perioperative ECLS may be considered according to patient and procedural risk; planned support and rescue ECMO are not interchangeable concepts
Reperfusion has no pulmonary vascular consequences
Transplant anesthetic management is standardized by one universally binding ventilator setting

practiceQuestions.rationale: Consensus and review sources describe high complexity and selective use of extracorporeal support, with no implication that all cases require it. The evidence does not justify a universal fixed plan.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult with a large anterior mediastinal mass has positional dyspnea and airway compression. Which plan element matters most?

options.text: Induce general anesthesia before assessing symptoms or imaging
Use a multidisciplinary, individualized airway and hemodynamic strategy with rescue options and contingency planning, recognizing that case reports are not universal protocols
Assume supine positioning improves all cases
Treat an online case report as a validated standard

practiceQuestions.rationale: Mediastinal mass can threaten airway and circulation during induction. Published reports illustrate hazards but do not create universal protocols; patient-specific planning, team readiness and specialist judgment are essential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner finds an image in NLM Open-i. What is the correct reuse rule for course materials?

options.text: NLM owns every image and grants blanket reuse rights
If viewable, it can be downloaded and redistributed
Link to the original source; assess each item’s displayed license and permissions before reuse, and do not copy patient images into this course
Remove identifying labels and the image becomes free to reuse

practiceQuestions.rationale: Open-i is a discovery resource, not a blanket license grant. De-identification and public viewing do not establish copyright permission; link-only use avoids unauthorized copying.

title: Cardiovascular Performance (Sports Cardiology) Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship / integrated nonstandard training pathways (not an independent accredited residency)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Postgraduate cardiology learner; intended for cardiology fellows, cardiologists and advanced clinicians with prior cardiovascular medicine knowledge. Not introductory medical training.
required: Medical degree and completion of foundational physician training appropriate to learner’s jurisdiction
Working knowledge of ECG, cardiovascular physiology and general cardiology
Access to current professional guidelines and a clinical supervisor for any real clinical application
notSubstitutes: Does not substitute for MD/DO education, ACGME-accredited cardiovascular disease fellowship, institutional sports-cardio training, supervised practice, clinical skills evaluation or continuing professional certification.

objectives: Explain the clinical rationale and limits of cardiovascular screening in athletes.
Interpret athlete ECG patterns with current criteria, context and appropriate uncertainty.
Distinguish physiological exercise-induced remodeling from cardiovascular pathology using multimodality evidence and longitudinal context.
Plan a supervised, clinically appropriate evaluation for symptoms, arrhythmia, abnormal imaging or reduced performance.
Discuss participation and return-to-sport questions through disease-specific evidence and shared decision-making.
Describe masters-athlete coronary prevention and exercise-testing considerations.
Appraise evidence for screening, diagnostic tests and athlete outcomes, including bias and equity.
Explain emergency action planning, privacy, image-use and educational scope limits.

units.title: Cardiovascular physiology, training load and athlete-centered history
objectives: Relate training volume/type and hemodynamic adaptation to cardiovascular physiology.
Elicit exertional symptoms, training history, medications/supplements, family history and goals without assuming fitness excludes disease.
Distinguish educational screening from diagnostic evaluation.
topics: Cardiac output, autonomic adaptation, remodeling continuum
Sport demands and training history
Symptoms, family history and risk context
boardDomains: Normal cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; preventive and rehabilitative cardiology
units.casePractice: Build a structured, fictional athlete history with red-flag symptoms, family history, sport-specific demands and next-step questions; do not provide a clearance decision from history alone.
units.assessment: One-page history/clinical-reasoning map; rubric: history completeness 40%, risk/context synthesis 30%, uncertainty and safety 30%.

units.title: Preparticipation cardiovascular screening and the limits of screening
objectives: Compare screening history/physical and ECG strategies, including trade-offs in detection, false positives, resources and follow-up.
Design a referral pathway for abnormal findings and symptoms.
Explain that screening has limits and is not a guarantee against sudden arrest.
topics: PPE cardiovascular history and examination
Population versus individual risk
ECG screening evidence and secondary evaluation
Equity, access, false positives and informed consent
boardDomains: Preventive/rehabilitative cardiology; sudden cardiac death; epidemiology and risk assessment
units.casePractice: Fictional collegiate program asks whether to add ECG screening; compare options and explain local resources/referral capacity without making blanket policy claims.
units.assessment: Evidence brief; rubric: evidence appraisal 35%, harms/benefits 25%, implementation safeguards 25%, communication 15%.

units.title: Athlete ECG: International Criteria and interpretation workflow
objectives: Use a systematic ECG reading sequence and distinguish common training-related patterns from findings warranting evaluation.
Identify age, sex, ethnicity/geographic-origin and sport context limitations.
Recognize that a normal ECG does not exclude all structural or exercise-triggered disorders.
topics: Sinus bradycardia, AV delay, isolated voltage, early repolarization
Pathological T-wave inversion, ST depression, pathological Q waves, pre-excitation and channelopathy patterns
Borderline findings, common interpretation errors and secondary evaluation
boardDomains: Arrhythmias; normal anatomy/physiology; ECG interpretation component
units.casePractice: Read only openly linked, consented PhysioNet ECG records under its license; waveform interpretation exercise is not a diagnosis and database has no structural imaging confirmation.
units.assessment: Blinded ECG reasoning worksheet; rubric: systematic acquisition 20%, classification/context 35%, differential and next tests 30%, uncertainty 15%.

units.title: Exercise-induced remodeling and multimodality imaging
objectives: Explain overlap between physiological remodeling and cardiomyopathy.
Select echocardiography, CMR or CT questions based on clinical hypothesis rather than modality availability.
Integrate training history, ECG, image phenotype and longitudinal change.
topics: Athlete’s heart: chamber size, wall thickness and function
Echo, CMR tissue characterization and coronary CT indications
Serial assessment, detraining questions and diagnostic uncertainty
boardDomains: Heart failure/cardiomyopathy; echo and imaging interpretation; coronary angiograms/CT contextual reasoning
units.casePractice: Use published open-access figures only by linking to the source; do not download, copy or redistribute figures unless the individual license permits.
units.assessment: Modality decision memo; rubric: question formulation 25%, modality limits 25%, integrated differential 30%, safety/communication 20%.

units.title: Hypertrophic, arrhythmogenic and dilated cardiomyopathy in active people
objectives: Construct a differential when ECG, imaging, symptoms or family history raise concern for cardiomyopathy.
Explain why athletic remodeling can mimic pathology and why no single metric settles all cases.
Identify when genetics, CMR, family assessment or specialist review may be appropriate.
topics: HCM versus physiological remodeling
Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and exercise exposure
Dilated/nonischemic cardiomyopathy, myocarditis scar and inherited disease
Family evaluation and longitudinal monitoring
boardDomains: Heart failure and cardiomyopathy (17% ABIM domain); ECG and echocardiogram interpretation
units.casePractice: Fictional athlete with exertional presyncope and equivocal structural findings; learners formulate differentials and state what evidence is missing.
units.assessment: Oral-board style case defense; rubric: differential 35%, test choice 25%, safety 20%, calibrated language 20%.

units.title: Arrhythmia, syncope, channelopathy and device considerations
objectives: Classify common athlete arrhythmia presentations and formulate an evidence-based evaluation plan.
Apply disease-specific risk assessment, not a blanket sports ban, to participation discussions.
Identify the emergency-planning and specialist inputs required for complex cases.
topics: Bradyarrhythmias, ectopy, SVT, AF and ventricular arrhythmias
Syncope, pre-excitation, long QT, Brugada and CPVT concepts
Ambulatory monitoring, exercise testing, inherited-arrhythmia assessment and ICD considerations
boardDomains: Arrhythmias (15% ABIM domain); ECG; pacemaker/ICD function; syncope and sudden cardiac death
units.casePractice: Fictional exertional palpitations/syncope case; map differential, red flags and testing; no treatment orders or clearance authorization.
units.assessment: Decision tree and 5-minute case presentation; rubric: prioritization 30%, evidence/domain accuracy 30%, participation caveats 25%, communication 15%.

units.title: Exercise physiology and cardiopulmonary exercise testing
objectives: Interpret CPET in relation to workload, protocol, effort, symptoms, ECG and gas-exchange signals.
Explain why protocol selection and termination thresholds must match clinical question and athlete context.
Recognize limitations and safety requirements of supervised testing.
topics: VO2, ventilatory thresholds, VE/VCO2, oxygen pulse and chronotropic response
Cycle/treadmill and sport-specific protocol choice
Exercise ECG, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, symptoms and recovery
Indications, contraindications, calibration and supervised conduct
boardDomains: Normal cardiovascular anatomy/physiology; preventive/rehabilitative cardiology; heart failure/cardiomyopathy
units.casePractice: Interpret a publicly documented teaching CPET if available; otherwise work a fictional, explicitly synthetic value table without representing it as patient data.
units.assessment: CPET interpretation note; rubric: signal interpretation 35%, physiology 25%, protocol/context 20%, limitations/safety 20%.

units.title: Masters athletes, coronary disease and preventive cardiology
objectives: Prioritize conventional coronary risk, age, symptoms and family history in masters-athlete evaluation.
Distinguish exercise benefit from absence of atherosclerotic risk.
Discuss testing and prevention within the applicable coronary-disease guidelines rather than routine indiscriminate imaging.
topics: Coronary disease in older athletes
Risk-factor optimization and symptom-triggered workup
Exercise-related event risk and baseline absolute risk
Coronary calcium/CT context and incidental findings
boardDomains: Coronary artery disease (21.5% ABIM domain); preventive cardiology; geriatric cardiovascular disease
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional masters-athlete profiles, accounting for symptoms and risk; avoid universal CT or stress-testing recommendations.
units.assessment: Risk communication letter; rubric: evidence/risk 35%, test reasoning 25%, shared decision-making 25%, plain language 15%.

units.title: Valve disease, congenital disease, aortopathy and myocarditis
objectives: Recognize athlete-specific questions arising from valve, congenital, aortic and inflammatory disease.
Identify high-risk features needing specialist evaluation before decisions about vigorous activity.
Use disease-specific current guidance and avoid extending one diagnosis’s participation rule to another.
topics: Aortic root and inherited aortopathy
Bicuspid aortic valve and valvular lesions
Congenital heart disease and repaired lesions
Myocarditis/pericarditis, recovery and return-to-exercise uncertainty
boardDomains: Valvular disease (15%); congenital heart disease (5%); pericardial disease; cardiomyopathy
units.casePractice: Build a problem representation from fictional findings; state the appropriate guideline date and which specialist decision is required.
units.assessment: Guideline-to-case matrix; rubric: correct domain 30%, current sourcing 30%, risk/uncertainty 25%, referral plan 15%.

units.title: Participation decisions, return to sport and shared decision-making
objectives: Use contemporary AHA/ACC and disease-specific recommendations as inputs to individualized participation discussions.
Communicate residual uncertainty, options, athlete preferences and consequences without coercion.
Document a collaborative plan that includes follow-up and emergency preparation.
topics: 2025 AHA/ACC statement structure and shared decision-making
Risk modifiers by disease, symptom, sport and testing
Athlete autonomy, family/coach roles, privacy and occupational/tactical settings
Return-to-sport follow-up and changing evidence
boardDomains: Risk assessment/prognosis; preventive/rehabilitative cardiology; ethics and communication
units.casePractice: Role-play fictional athlete/family/team conversation; no real patient advice or guaranteed clearance.
units.assessment: Structured shared-decision-making encounter; rubric: accurate options 30%, elicitation of goals 25%, balanced uncertainty 25%, documentation 20%.

units.title: Sudden cardiac arrest prevention, emergency action plans and event medicine
objectives: Describe the role of prompt recognition, emergency activation, CPR/AED access and rehearsed emergency action planning.
Identify athlete-event symptoms requiring emergency response rather than continuation of activity.
Separate prevention planning from prediction of individual sudden arrest.
topics: Cardiac arrest recognition and response systems
Emergency action plans, AED placement/access and drills
Event medical coordination, exertional collapse differential, heat illness overlap
Post-event review and quality improvement
boardDomains: Sudden cardiac death; arrhythmias; critical care and systems-based practice
units.casePractice: Tabletop review of fictional venue plan; use current local emergency response protocol and certified CPR/AED instruction for actual skills.
units.assessment: EAP gap analysis; rubric: response sequence 35%, team/system design 30%, role clarity 20%, debrief plan 15%.

units.title: Research methods, equity, communication and lifelong learning
objectives: Critically appraise screening/test-performance studies, selection bias, prevalence, outcomes and external validity.
Recognize limits of demographic labels and strive for equitable ECG interpretation and access.
Build a personal evidence update process and distinguish education from credentialing.
topics: Study design, diagnostic accuracy, bias and outcome ascertainment
Shared registry/QI principles and privacy
Diversity, sex, age, sport type and geographic-origin considerations
Practice improvement, professional scope and source currency
boardDomains: Epidemiology, prevention, health equity, professionalism and systems-based practice
units.casePractice: Appraise a published screening paper and dataset; state who is missing and what database cannot establish.
units.assessment: Evidence appraisal and 1-page QI proposal; rubric: methods 35%, bias/equity 25%, feasibility 20%, ethics/privacy 20%.

assignment.title: Capstone: athlete cardiovascular evaluation and shared-decision case conference
assignment.instructions: Prepare one fictional, clearly labeled athlete case and give a 12-minute presentation plus a 2-page evidence note. Include sport/training context, symptoms and history, ECG/imaging/CPET reasoning as applicable, differential, what evidence is missing, guideline date, risks/benefits and a shared-decision conversation. Use linked source material only; no real patient details, copied private records, or unauthorized images. Do not prescribe or provide a real person with clearance.
deliverables: Fictional case summary and focused history
One annotated evidence-based test/interpretation pathway
Two-option participation discussion with uncertainty and follow-up
One-page references and rights statement

rubric.criterion: Case privacy, image rights and citations

assignment.passingInterpretation: Formative scoring only; no validated board-passing predictor or clinical competence determination.

assessment.format: Ten original single-best-answer questions plus unit worksheets, case discussion and capstone. They are original educational items, not official examination questions and not a validated exam predictor.
assessment.feedback: Review every rationale and primary source. Errors indicate topics to revisit, not a score-based eligibility or clinical readiness statement.

rubric.criterion: Case privacy, image rights and citations

studyHours.description: Suggested 120-hour self-study plan: approximately 36 hours of currently verified public lecture video target, 36 hours of primary reading, 24 hours of case/ECG/CPET reasoning and 24 hours of revision, writing and question review. Only 0.4103 hours of the 36 video target is presently verified. The remaining 35.5897 hours are not study completion and not video delivered; they are a content acquisition/production gap. Learners may use the readings/cases, but those do not count as lecture video hours.

topicGaps: After adding 23 unique recordings, 7.1397 actual accessible, free, duration-verified hours are counted (unique canonical media IDs; the existing 24:37 Mayo lecture is included); 28.8603 hours remain to the 36-hour video floor. This gap is not study completion or delivered media.

The EAPC 2024 recorded course and Cardiac Risk in the Young 2026 public lectures add focused material in ECG, athlete imaging, screening, arrhythmia, ICD, cardiac arrest, equity, and fibrosis. Individual runtimes were obtained from publicly exposed player/playlist metadata and watch pages, without authentication or bypass. The 5:33 opening orientation is excluded as non-teaching.

No dedicated long-form verified recording was found for detailed CPET protocol/interpretation, myocarditis/pericarditis recovery, congenital heart disease, valve/aortic disease, disease-specific sports participation across the full curriculum, or robust research-methods instruction. Unit 9 is especially undercovered by verified media; the readings and official statements are not video hours.

The public recordings are a small selection of conference talks, not a complete course, and several are older or short. Their total cannot substantiate all 36 hours. Check current primary guidance; no public institutional case portfolio, direct-observation competency evidence, or institutional training outcome is claimed.

The unresolved Mayo master's-athlete video remains uncounted because the public page shows 00:00 / 00:00 and no observed runtime. No protected course, member-only content, or paywall-gated recording was counted.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship / integrated nonstandard training pathways (not an independent accredited residency)
boardNames: ABIM Cardiovascular Disease Certification Examination (underlying general cardiovascular disease board; eligibility is governed solely by ABIM requirements and completed training)
No separate U.S. sports-cardiology board certification or specialty examination identified in the 2025 curriculum review (checked 2026-10-07)
medical.boardStatus: Sports cardiology is a genuine physician clinical subspecialty field with institutional advanced/integrated training pathways, but the 2025 scholarly review reports no ACGME-accredited sports-cardiology fellowship and no separate sports-cardiology board certification. The MGB CPP is an institution-listed one-year advanced program after general cardiology fellowship; Hopkins describes sports cardiology as integrated in its cardiovascular disease fellowship, not a stand-alone program. Underlying cardiovascular disease board certification is distinct.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course does not confer board eligibility, exam eligibility, accreditation, institutional affiliation or clinical credentials. MGB lists completion of three years of ACGME-accredited cardiovascular disease fellowship as its prerequisite; Hopkins describes an integrated trainee pathway. Current applicants must confirm eligibility and requirements directly with institutions and ABIM. No board passing or eligibility claim is made.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass General Brigham (program administratively housed at Massachusetts General Hospital)
officialProgrammes.name: Cardiovascular Performance Program Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a one-year advanced training program for cardiologists, requires successful completion of three years of an ACGME-accredited cardiovascular disease fellowship, and reports four curricular rotations/domains: clinical athlete care, research methodology, pre-participation screening and advanced exercise testing/physiology, with weekly didactics and direct observation/case portfolio. These are program claims, not independently verified training outcomes or hours.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins Medicine
officialProgrammes.name: Sports Cardiology Fellowship (integrated pathway)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page explicitly says sports cardiology is integrated into the broader Cardiovascular Disease Fellowship and is not a stand-alone fellowship or separate application. Lists sports clinics, diagnostic testing, case discussions, pre-participation screening and CPET experiences. Hopkins-affiliated 2025 curriculum article describes a nonstandard training pathway; partner sites are also named.

medical.programmeSourceScope: These are institutional training descriptions, not an ACGME program directory, a public institutional lecture inventory, a validated curriculum, or verification of accreditation. Johns Hopkins partner organizations listed on its official page include University of Maryland Medical Center, Cardiovascular Specialists of Central Maryland and Sports & Performance Cardiology; the exact institutional track is integrated with Hopkins CVD fellowship.
sourceCaveats: Institutional pages can change and do not independently verify accreditation or training outcomes.

The 2025 curriculum review is the most direct source found for absence of a U.S. sports-cardio ACGME fellowship and separate board certification. This is a date-bound statement; re-check ABMS, ACGME and boards before reuse.

ABIM general cardiovascular disease exam blueprint is only a parent-specialty study mapping; it is not a sports-cardio exam. Board eligibility depends on ABIM and underlying accredited training rules.
Johns Hopkins page describes a clinical training pathway integrated into CVD fellowship and not a stand-alone sports-cardio fellowship; do not conflate with MGB CPP one-year offering.
The open athlete ECG dataset has 28 recordings and no structural imaging assessment; it cannot validate cardiomyopathy/no-disease diagnosis.
The HRS PubMed abstract is accessible; publisher full text was not established as free. The AHA page is a summary and may link to publisher-restricted full text.
No authentic patient images or records were copied. Institutional case conference/clinic volumes and unpublished teaching materials are unavailable and not claimed.
Human clinical review has not been performed; all care decisions require qualified clinical oversight.

topicGaps: After adding 23 unique recordings, 7.1397 actual accessible, free, duration-verified hours are counted (unique canonical media IDs; the existing 24:37 Mayo lecture is included); 28.8603 hours remain to the 36-hour video floor. This gap is not study completion or delivered media.

The EAPC 2024 recorded course and Cardiac Risk in the Young 2026 public lectures add focused material in ECG, athlete imaging, screening, arrhythmia, ICD, cardiac arrest, equity, and fibrosis. Individual runtimes were obtained from publicly exposed player/playlist metadata and watch pages, without authentication or bypass. The 5:33 opening orientation is excluded as non-teaching.

No dedicated long-form verified recording was found for detailed CPET protocol/interpretation, myocarditis/pericarditis recovery, congenital heart disease, valve/aortic disease, disease-specific sports participation across the full curriculum, or robust research-methods instruction. Unit 9 is especially undercovered by verified media; the readings and official statements are not video hours.

The public recordings are a small selection of conference talks, not a complete course, and several are older or short. Their total cannot substantiate all 36 hours. Check current primary guidance; no public institutional case portfolio, direct-observation competency evidence, or institutional training outcome is claimed.

The unresolved Mayo master's-athlete video remains uncounted because the public page shows 00:00 / 00:00 and no observed runtime. No protected course, member-only content, or paywall-gated recording was counted.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 19-year-old asymptomatic rower has sinus bradycardia and isolated increased QRS voltage meeting LVH voltage criteria; examination and family history are unremarkable. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: These findings alone prove hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
They can be training-related findings under athlete ECG criteria; interpret in context and assess any red flags.
The athlete should be permanently excluded from sport.
A normal ECG excludes all important cardiovascular disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Sinus bradycardia and isolated voltage criteria for LVH can be common training-related findings. ECG is interpreted with symptoms, family history, morphology and applicable athlete criteria; it neither diagnoses HCM alone nor rules out all disease.

practiceQuestions.stem: A young athlete has one borderline ECG finding and no symptoms. Under the International Criteria framework, which principle is most accurate?

options.text: Any borderline feature is automatically pathological.
One borderline finding is always normal regardless of context.
Borderline findings are interpreted as a group; two or more borderline features prompt further evaluation under the stated criteria, with context still essential.
No testing is ever appropriate if the athlete competes.

practiceQuestions.rationale: International Criteria distinguish normal, borderline and abnormal findings; the review reports that two or more borderline findings warrant further evaluation. Clinical context and exact criteria matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects limitations of a normal resting athlete ECG?

options.text: It excludes anomalous coronary anatomy, CPVT and all cardiomyopathies.
It cannot exclude all structural disease or exercise-triggered electrical disease; symptoms may warrant further evaluation.
It predicts no future event with certainty.
It eliminates the need for history and examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Resting ECG has known sensitivity limitations. Some substrates or exercise-induced arrhythmias may not be apparent at rest, and clinical symptoms require attention.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 54-year-old marathon runner reports exertional chest pressure. What is the most appropriate initial reasoning?

options.text: Training history makes coronary disease implausible.
Treat this as a symptom requiring standard clinical evaluation and coronary risk assessment; do not offer blanket reassurance from fitness.
Order coronary CT in every masters athlete, regardless of symptoms.
Clear for racing because exercise is cardioprotective.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Physical activity benefits health but does not abolish coronary disease or symptoms. Evaluation is individualized and informed by current coronary guidelines, risk and clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about U.S. sports cardiology fellowship/board status is correct as of the source review (2025) and current institutional pages checked Oct 7 2026?

options.text: Sports cardiology has an ACGME-accredited fellowship and separate ABIM board exam.
Sports cardiology training pathways exist, including MGB advanced training and Hopkins integrated experience, but there is no separate sports-cardiology board certification identified.
Johns Hopkins describes its program as a stand-alone application outside cardiology fellowship.
An independent online course makes a learner board-eligible.

practiceQuestions.rationale: MGB describes a one-year advanced program after cardiovascular fellowship; Hopkins says its sports experience is integrated into cardiovascular disease fellowship. Published 2025 curriculum article states no ACGME sports-cardio fellowship and no sports-cardio board exam.

practiceQuestions.stem: A physically active adult presents after exertional syncope. Which is the safest learning-level action?

options.text: Assume a benign training adaptation.
Use urgent clinical evaluation and disease-specific assessment; a case discussion cannot issue clearance.
Recommend immediate self-directed maximal testing.
Use only a wearable device to exclude arrhythmia.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Syncope during exertion is a potentially important symptom; evaluation requires qualified clinical assessment and appropriate testing. This educational scenario gives no treatment or clearance advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which test is best chosen for an athlete with exertional symptoms and reduced exercise tolerance?

options.text: A fixed one-size-fits-all exercise protocol irrespective of sport or clinical question.
A supervised exercise/CPET strategy selected for the clinical question, symptoms, sport and safety context.
No exercise testing is ever appropriate in an athlete.
A maximal test performed without medical supervision.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Curricula emphasize supervised CPET, protocol selection and interpretation in context. This does not authorize unsupervised testing; test indications depend on clinician judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about PhysioNet Norwegian Endurance Athlete ECG database is supported by its documentation?

options.text: It contains 28 athletes with ECG plus echo-proven cardiomyopathy ground truth.
It contains 28 consented athlete ECG recordings and carries CC BY 4.0; no echocardiographic examination established structural diagnoses.
The ECG data are proprietary and unavailable.
Its algorithm labels are a definitive clinical diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: PhysioNet describes 28 athlete ECGs, participant consent, CC BY 4.0, and explicitly says no echo/other examinations assessed cardiac structure. The records support education, not diagnostic labels.

practiceQuestions.stem: During an athlete participation discussion, the most evidence-aligned communication approach is:

options.text: Prohibit participation for all cardiovascular diagnoses without discussion.
Use current condition-specific evidence, communicate risks and uncertainty, and engage in shared decision-making.
Promise zero risk after a negative test.
Let the coach alone determine medical risk.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 AHA/ACC statement emphasizes clinical considerations and shared decision-making. No single test guarantees safety; decisions should be individualized and clinician-led.

practiceQuestions.stem: A sports event reviews its cardiac emergency readiness. Which item belongs in an emergency action plan?

options.text: Only annual ECG screening.
Clear recognition/activation roles, accessible AED/CPR response, practice/drills and review of local emergency procedures.
A guarantee no athlete will arrest.
No plan unless a prior event occurred.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Consensus and training sources emphasize emergency preparedness and action planning. Actual CPR/AED skills require recognized practical training; this course does not certify resuscitation competence.

deliverables: Fictional 2-page presentation/problem representation and diagnostic question, distinguishing chronic symptomatic PAD, CLTI, ALI or venous differential.

rubric.meetsStandard: Identifies the likely syndrome without overclaiming; recognizes red flags and appropriate urgency.
Selects tests tied to a question; integrates discordance and limitations.

Uses fictional or linked cases only; no copied images or real patient identifiers; disclaims training/credential claims.

topicGaps: Verified free, public-page vascular recordings add 4.975 hours; the target is 36 hours, leaving 31.025 actual hours of verified external-video gap. The four counted recordings have observed public player runtimes; playback itself was not streamed during this stateless review.

Substantial specialist-specific deficits remain in noninvasive physiologic interpretation and waveform integration, arterial duplex and CTA/MRA/DSA limitations, current PAD prevention/antithrombotic decisions, CLTI/WIfI/GLASS and limb preservation, ALI mechanisms and urgent pathways, venous DVT probability pathways and chronic reflux/obstruction, carotid/upper-extremity/aortic/renal/mesenteric disease, intervention decision science and post-intervention surveillance.

Four new candidate recordings (CLTI decision-making, PAD BootCamp episode 2, 2024 PAD guideline navigation, and Michigan PAD treatment strategies) remain uncounted because exact player runtimes and/or free-playback evidence were not exposed. Existing candidate records remain preserved.

Five original episodes are fully scripted but not rendered; their spoken duration is not counted. The existing 36-hour originalClipPlan remains a production plan, not media. No video generated or uploaded; future production remains needed for the residual gap.

No standalone vascular diagnostic/intervention board is named by the MGH listing. Separate ABVM examination/credential requirements and RPVI scope remain distinct; no course or video hours confer eligibility, certification, procedural competency, or supervised training.

medical.boardStatus: The named fellowship is a physician postgraduate clinical fellowship listed by MGB; the official listing does not name a separate board examination or state ACGME accreditation. As of 2026-10-07, Inteleos/APCA separately lists ABVM Vascular and ABVM Endovascular examinations/certification tracks; eligibility is controlled by that certifier and is not conferred by this MGH listing or course. RPVI/PVI is an ultrasound-interpretation credential, not an independent physician specialty board. ABIM cardiovascular disease is an adjacent distinct board examination; the MGH fellowship requires completed cardiovascular disease fellowship or equivalent, but does not claim itself as an ABIM qualifying program.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: No standalone vascular diagnostic/intervention board examination is named by the official MGH programme page. The separate ABVM exams and RPVI credential have individual current prerequisites administered by APCA/Inteleos; eligibility is not assumed. ABIM Cardiovascular Disease certification has separate requirements, including qualifying accredited CV fellowship training. Verify directly with certifier before reliance.

officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page says training in noninvasive vascular diagnostics and catheter-based vascular interventions; PAD, venous disease and vascular imaging; noninvasive vascular lab (duplex and physiologic testing), peripheral arterial angiography/intervention, venous assessment/treatment, CTA/MRA interpretation, outpatient vascular clinics. Entry requirement stated as completed cardiovascular disease fellowship or equivalent. Page does not state programme duration, ACGME accreditation, full syllabus, exact rotations/calendar, procedure/case minimum, board eligibility or credential award.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The official MGH page is the primary source. The SVM directory lists a separate MGH Clinical Vascular Medicine Fellowship and separate BWH/VA Boston Interventional Vascular Medicine Fellowship; those institutional tracks are not merged as variants. MGB specialty directory inclusion is evidence of listing, not evidence of ACGME accreditation. The track is a clinical physician fellowship, not generic vascular surgery/interventional radiology, not a research-only postdoctoral programme, and not a non-physician ultrasound supplement. SCAI 2023 reports advanced PVI fellowship training was not ACGME-accredited at time of its publication; the programme page itself does not state current accreditation, so no current accreditation inference is made.
sourceCaveats: MGH programme page lists a clinical physician fellowship and states the CV fellowship/equivalent entry requirement; exact current accreditation and duration are not publicly stated there.

The separate MGH clinical vascular medicine fellowship, BWH/VA Boston interventional vascular medicine fellowship, and vascular/endovascular surgery training programmes remain distinct, not merged as MGH fellowship variants.

ABVM Vascular/Endovascular are separate APCA-administered certification pathways; RPVI is a physician ultrasound interpretation credential. None is automatically conferred by this curriculum or fellowship listing.

The specific directory label does not establish ACGME status. SCAI 2023 article says advanced PVI fellowship training was not ACGME-accredited at that time; current MGH programme status was not confirmed.

Search surfaced several candidate vascular recordings, but stateless YouTube metadata extraction could not retrieve player responses. Their runtimes, free accessibility and full content are therefore unknown and none is counted. One other search result led to a login-only course and was excluded.
The 2024 multisociety PAD guideline and 2025 SVS claudication guidance were checked as of 2026-10-07. Clinical decisions should use live current guidance and local protocols.
The MGH listing does not publish exact rotations, case or procedure numbers, completion outcomes, or formal board eligibility. No such facts are invented.
Radiopaedia is free-to-view but this does not grant broad rehosting rights. Use link-only case access, check per-case licence/terms/attribution, and do not copy images or patient records.

topicGaps: Verified free, public-page vascular recordings add 4.975 hours; the target is 36 hours, leaving 31.025 actual hours of verified external-video gap. The four counted recordings have observed public player runtimes; playback itself was not streamed during this stateless review.

Substantial specialist-specific deficits remain in noninvasive physiologic interpretation and waveform integration, arterial duplex and CTA/MRA/DSA limitations, current PAD prevention/antithrombotic decisions, CLTI/WIfI/GLASS and limb preservation, ALI mechanisms and urgent pathways, venous DVT probability pathways and chronic reflux/obstruction, carotid/upper-extremity/aortic/renal/mesenteric disease, intervention decision science and post-intervention surveillance.

Four new candidate recordings (CLTI decision-making, PAD BootCamp episode 2, 2024 PAD guideline navigation, and Michigan PAD treatment strategies) remain uncounted because exact player runtimes and/or free-playback evidence were not exposed. Existing candidate records remain preserved.

Five original episodes are fully scripted but not rendered; their spoken duration is not counted. The existing 36-hour originalClipPlan remains a production plan, not media. No video generated or uploaded; future production remains needed for the residual gap.

No standalone vascular diagnostic/intervention board is named by the MGH listing. Separate ABVM examination/credential requirements and RPVI scope remain distinct; no course or video hours confer eligibility, certification, procedural competency, or supervised training.
